0 WINDS. 0 winds, touch tenderly the leaves that cling But by a thread unto the parent tree: A breath of froit will softly set them free, . And earth will cfaht them for her ministering. ; And oh, fall gently leaves that once did sing For wealth of life and joyous greenery, With no forecastings of the dark To Be, When winter must eclipse the dowers of spring. 0 Earth, thy bosom waits for many a gift, Be gentle as to those whom Beauty.led From change to change, and day by day had fed With silver4lgbt3 of dew. Will thy veil lift 7- To-show us radiant life restored and blessed? Ali, then, ah then, no beauty shall be missed. Welcome.

• .. JUBILEE HYMN. •. .3.r04z1 For all thy countless bounties, Through varied chance and change; For old familiar blefaings, • For mercies new and strange For laws that widen slowly, - _ For ordered life and free; . . We thank Thee. Lord, and welcome ]sr•Lo . Our year of Jubilee. • For queenly wisdom, sought:for In prayer of early days; . For guidance pure and noble, That won the wide world's praise; 1" For children taught to follow , Their father's footsteps true; • •7 ' For after-glow of brightness; We now our thanks renew. -- • • ' For peace with all her triumphs, • ' Peace welcomed after war; For prosperous years that brought us - Rich gifts from near and far; For days of darker outlook, ' That tried the nation's nerve; For all alike we thank Thee; • • 'thou gav'st ; Thou canst preserve. .. • For onward march of knowledge, ' That grows from more to more; For words of noblest wisdom -- From poet's golden lore; For these we praise Thee, Father. Oh, make us Sons of Light, Against the hosts of darkness; With these, for Thee, to fight! The fifty years behind us Have told their wondrous tale; • : The fifty years before us Lie yet within the veil; . Grant, Lord, that all our future sr, May work out good begun ; That, in the tasks that wait us, The goal at last be won! . Tfirough all Thy saints and servants, Send forth Thy Light and Truth; . • •. Renew our nation's greatness,. As 'twere an eagle's youth: " So. with full hearts of gladness, - We lift our souls to Thee, And keep in hope and courage, Our_Year of Jubilee. Amen. —Dean Ptuntire, in Good ,Words.

In the course of James'Vl.'s progress from Edinburgh th London, when he went to assume the sovereignity of his new empire ho was treated with a splendid entertain- ment by a mayor of an English town, whose liberality was such that he kept open house, in honour of the new sovereign, for several days. Some of the English courtiers -took occasion from this to hint that such examples of munificence must be very rare among the civic digni- taries of a certain other kingdom. "Feint a bit o' that are they !" cried King James, "The provost o' my burgh e' Forfar, vvhilk is by nae means the largest, town in Scotland, keeps open house a' the year round, and aye the mae that comes the welcomer !" The secret was that, the chief magistrate of Forfar 'kept an ale- house. THE WREN AND rise ROBIN.—And the wren, what a bewitching little morsel it looks, when in the leafless publicity of winter it hops about in the empty bushes or perches itself, wee dwarf in feathers, on the wall. Yet within its small person, so tradition alleges, it holds necromantic potentialities of a very serious kind, •and en one occasion at least wasthe abiding-place of Beelze- bub himself. Poor little mite! you do not look like it, skipping in and out my old pea-sticks, and suddenly stoppingiu your elfin antics to trill a roundelay. • And the robin up in the medlar-tree listens. He is lord of the garden croft; but he turns his shapely head—how the round black eye glistens—and waits till the wren has finished, and then gives a stave of his own. What gentleman he is' this robin of ours, always elegant. always self-possessed. You can never see without re- specting bins. Ms every gesture is in good taste, and musicians say his song is singularly correct. Most punctilious as to his honour, he is ready 'to draw his sword at the first hint of insult, anti when with his equals, his hand is perpetually clapped to his side, a veritable little fire-eater among his peers, attacking with the light-hearted dash, and pursuing with the gallant recklessness of a Cavalier. And yet, when the etiquette ef robinhood is not infringed, he is a delightfully well- bred little person, coming into your presence with an unassuming, self-respectful independence that is very engaging, and leaving, when he has said what he has to say, with the same ease of bearing, the same unaffected demeanour.—Phil Robinson, in "Good ,W7ds." He says—"l confine the advertising of my soap to the newspapers, because the man who does not read the newspapers doeantit usesoap."- Tux SIGILL OF WARDLEY HALL, WORSLEY.—AV ,Ward- ley Hall, an ancient mansion in Worsley, there is said to be a skull with a history attached to it. Mr. Thomas Wardle, who visited the house at the close of last cen- tury, says there is a tradition that, "if removed or used, some uncommon noise or disturbance always follows, to the terror of the whole house. Yet I cannot persuade myself that this is always the case; but some years ago, I and three of my companions went to visit thiT surprising piece of household furniture, and found it as above-mentioned, and blanched white with weather that beats upon it from it four-square window in the hall, which the tenants never permit to be glazed or filled up; thus to oblige the skull, which they say is'un- ruly and disturbed at the hole not always being open. However, one of as who was last in company of the skull removed it from its place into a dark part of the room, and there left it anctreturned home. But the night but one following,, such a storm of wind and lightning rose about the house as tore down some trees and un- roofed onthouses. We hearing of this, my father went over to see his mother, who lived near- the hall, and was witness to the wreck the storm had made: Yet all this; might have been stopped had the skull -never been re- moved; but withal it keeps alive the credulity of its believers. What I can learn of the above affair from old people in the neighbourhood is that a young man of the Downes family, being in London, one ni ;lit in his frolic vowed to his companions that he wonld kill the first man he met. Accordinglyhe ran his sword through a man, a sailor by trade. Justice, however, overtook Him in his career of wickedness, for in some while after, he being in riot upon London Bridge, a watchman made a stroke at him with his bill, and severed his head from his body. The head was enclosed in a box and sent to his sister, Who lived at Wardley, where it hath continued ever since."—All the Yearßound._ • • • THE' EARLY LIFE OF ABRAHAM LINCOLTL—He had only been six months at school when his father was "cleaned out," through having to pay a bill which he had endorsed for a friend. Abe had to "go and hire himself out." that the produce of his labour might help the family funds. He was never at school again, and what further education lie gained was in reading "all , the books he ever heard of in the country for a circuit of ' fifty miles." When he was nineteen the family migrated to Illinois, and shortly afterwards Abraham left home with all his worldly possessions tied up in a handkerchief slung over his shoulder. Tramping over the prairies along an old Indian trail. he reached Macon County, where he found some cousins called Hanks, with whom he engaged in "splitting rails" at so much per hundred. Then he drifted into a fresh neighbourhood, and he took employment under a farmer. While worgihe in Sanga- mon County he was struck with the difficylty the farmers had in getting their produce:to market, afid he conceived the idea of building a flat boat upon the Sangamon river, running it down thence into Illinois, thence into the Mississippi, and so to New Orleans. Ho also devised a method of surmounting a dam, which formed an obstacle in this long waterway. He felled the timber, built the boat, loaded it, and went in charge of it as "captain." with a crew of two men, one of them being Hanks. Two or three years Lincoln worked in this boat, and then he became " clerk " in a store in the town of New Salem, in Sangamon County, in which was sold "a very few goods of various kinds." He shortly became a partner in this concern, but soon left again, in consequence of a dispute about whisky. The oia proprietor wanted to keep a cask toi "Invite custom." but Lincoln wouldn't have it. "lie told me,' writes Mr. Leonard Swett, "not more than a year :before he was elected President, that he had never tasted liquor in his life. 'What,' I said, 'do you mean to, say you never, tasted it?' Yes, I never tasted it.' The result was that Lincoln dissolved the partnership, the partner taking all the goods and agreeing to pay all the debts. But instead of paying the debts he took to drink, and when Lincoln came back to the place, after serving as captain of a company of volunteers in an expedition against the Indians, he found' that he was liable for some eleven hundred dollars. "I cannot forget," says Mr. Swett, "his face of seriousness as he turned to me and said, 'That debt was the greatest obstacle I ever met in lifer. I had no way of speculating, and could not earn money except by labour; and to earn by labour eleven hundred dollars, besides my living, seemed the work of a lifetime. There was, however, but one way. I went to the creditors, and told them if they would let me alone, I would give them all I could earn over my living as fast as I could earn it." And by hard work.and economy he paid it off in the course of a few years. Pate was kind to him, for about this time he got employment in the c'oun'y surveyoe.s office, and four years later was elected member of the State legis- lature. This meant at that time four dollars a day of allowance, "and four dollars a day," said Lincoln, "was more than T had ever earned in my life before." This was the beginning of his political career, for in the Illinois legislature his natural gift for public speaking developed itself, and what we may call his education in public affairs rapidly advanced. Of 'other education, Mr. Swett says, f' Life was to him a school, and he was always studying and mastering every subject whieli came before him. He knew how to dig out any question from its very roots, and when his own children began to go to school, he studied with them and aequired in mature life the elements of an education. I have seen him myself upon the circuit, with a geometry' or an astro- nomy.' or some book of that •kind, working out proposi- tions in moments of leisure, or acquiring the information that is generally acquired in boyhood." After serving his term in the State legislature, Lincoln went to Spring- field and began to study law. He rose in his new pro- fession, we are told, with great rapidity, and soon be- came a leader in it. It was while practising as'a lawyer at Springfield that Abraham Lincoln was elected Presi- dent. of the United States.—All the Year baud. LIBERAL BALL AT WARRINGTON.

The Liberal boll, which has bees looked forward to with some interest for several weeks, was held on Tuesday evening, in the Assembly Room at the Lion Hotel, and proved, as was anticipated, a_very enjoyable event. The room had been very hand- ' somely decorated by Mrs. O'Brien, to whom the work had been entrusted by Miss Hart, the manageress of the Lion Hotel. It was gay on every side with trophies and flags, which were skilfully, and taste- fully, arranged, and had a capital effect. No doubt it a few large mirrors had been added the effect would have been still further enhanced. The floor ! had, as usual, been carefully prepared, and was pro- nounced by the dancers to be in the best condition.' Instead of making use of the orchestra at the end of the room, which from its position would have IT- suited in some of the music- being lost, a temporary platform was erected just beneath it, and, being suitably adorned, it was found to be., very appropriate for the occasion. The music was discoursed by Mr. R. H. Pearson's band, and it is scarcely necessary to say that it gave the utmost satisfaction. The music was, as it ought to be, lively and varied, and of a modern character, as will be seen by the following programme:—Waltz, " Queenie ;" lancers, "Jollity;" waltz; "With the stream:" polka, "Secret marriage e' waltz; "Lily I Queen:" schottische," Marie Stuart;" waltz, °‘ Me- I laide ;" quadrille, "Pantomime:" waltz "Love's dreamland ;" quadrille, "Merry England:"Mazurka, " Violette ;" lancers, " Mikado ;" waltz, "Epigram," schottische, "Immerwieder ;" lancers, " Citrmener ' waltz, "./gioisette." Dancing commenced at 8-30„ and WAS continued with great spirit, with a very short interval, until 2,30 in the morning..- The out and out lovers of the Terpsichorean art had nothing to complain of, as their wishes were especially considered in drawing up a list of dances. The waltz, including the "extras " dining sup- per hour, Came with almost redundant frequency, and its "linked sweetness" was, besides, "long drawn out." If we might venture a suggestion we would say that on the next occasiotir opportunity should not be given for anyone to say. "-Sbmething too much df this." Supper was laid In the Coffee- roam of the hotel, and it included, every delicacy of the season. It was served in MiseHertlf best style, and gave universal satisfaction. Ample provision was made in the various ante-rooms for the com- fort and convenience of the ladies and gentlemen' attending the ball, and provision was also made. for light refreshment being supplied throughout the evening. Mr. F. A. Roberts acted as Master of the Ceremonies, and the stewards were Messrs. Thomas Morris, J. J. Crosfleld, J. IL Fleming, Thomas Birc- hall. and Henry Roberts. Mr. Arthur Browne acted as honorary secretary, and upon him, of course, devolved much of the labour attendant upon prepar- ing for the ball. It is due to all the officials to say that they were attentive to their dutie_s_, and that the proceedings were carried out without a single hitch. Stockport.— ' Arbt • Men talk much of the right of free speech and con- demn all attempts to fetter it. They should also respect the right of free silence, and visit with equal censure all attempts to violate it by inconsiderate and unbenevolent questioning prompted by curiosity. Men and women are not like leaves, blown about by every wind; or like clay, receiving and retaining what- ever impress is made upon them. They have an inward farce, enabling them to control to a large extent the in- fluences that bear upon them—to welcome some, to resist others, and not only passively to receive, but actively to digest and to assimilate that which they receive, so that it becomes a very part of themselves. div.p: OPENING OF PARLIAMENT. THE QUEEN'S SPEECH.
HOUSE OF LORDS.—THuRsDLY.

, be carried out, and therefore he could not retain his place in a Government in which effective retrenchment found no prominent place. The average expenditere of the army and navy for ten years was twenty-five millions; but in recent vests it had risen from twenty-five to thirty-one mil- lions. That was no light matter, and he only requested his colleagues to make an appreciable effort at reduction. When he found that they would not make a commencement of retrenchment he resigned. He oelieved that if the pelicy of the country were peaceful these Estimates were too great. He felt equally certain that at this moment the policy of the country ought to be a genuinely peaceful policy that would approach to non-intervention. It was said that he resigned in haste or in temper; but the fact was the difference en that subject with his colleagues had been going on al- most from the commencement of the Government. He read his letter of resignation to Lord Salisbury, pointing out how strongly be was apposed to the estimates presented by Mr. W. H. Smith and Lord George Hamilton, that he was cer- tain he could find no supporters in the Cabinet, and that as he did not want wrangling there he must request to be allowed to retire. He' was Pledged to a large reduction of exoenditare, and he could not change his mind on the subject. Lord Salisbury wrote in reply that the expenditure proposed was necessary for the defence of the coaling stations. Lord Salisbury ex- pressed full concurrence in it, remarking that it was not too enrich to say that the chances were in favour of war at an early date. He (Lord R. Churchill) replied that he declined to be a party to join in the high and desperate stakes that other nations were playing for Mr. W. H. &urn declared on the part of the Government that there was a desire io keep England out of unnecessary complicationr, and not to enter into any engagonent which would tie the hands of the Government. As to taxation, he was conscious of the suffering the taxpayers had had to endure, and if it should be found possible to effect a re- duction of the public burdens he would be the first to wel- come assistance in that direction, from whatever part of the House it might proceed. DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS. The Addrese in reply to the Speech from the Throne was moved by Lord WEverourn and seconded by Mr. G. W. Reaxourt.—ln the course of a long criticism, Mr. GLAD. BToNE, referring to Ireland, said he gathered from the Queen's Speech that with the Government the question of local Government in Ireland was a shadow and a dream. His opinions were fully placed on record when he proposed the Local Government Bill of the ' late Government, and to those opinions he en- tirely adhered. As to the reference to the organised attempt to incite occupiers to evade their legal- ' obligations, he thought the evictions in Ireland had pro duced a profound sensation in this country, and it would have been well to express some regret that it was found necessary to proceed in the depth of winter to evict by force 1 from their houses people of whom there was no evidence that they were able to pay their rents. He was asked he opinion of the plan of campaign, and he would give it. The plan of campaign was a consequence of the policy that the Government and their friends had pursued. He defended the efforts made last session to stay evictions, and pointed out that after the Conservative party had denied that the tenants were unable to pay their rents it was under- stood that the Chief Secretary for Ireland had been putting pressure upon the landlords. It was the policy of the Go- vernment that led to those deplorable proceedings, which tended to compromise the dignity of the law, and which bad caused a thrill of horror throughout the country.—Mr. W. ' H. Smith, Mr. W. Redmond, Mr. J. O'Connor, and other members took part in the debate.—Colonel Sannderson moved its adjournment.—The motion was agreed to and the House rose at 12-20 a.m.

- 1 The second session of the twelfth Parliament of Queen Victoria, and the twenty-fourth of Great Britain and Ire- land, was opened by Royal Commission on Thursday after- noon. The House of Lords threw open its doors at noon, although the ceremony of opening Parliament Was not to take place until two o'clock. Long before two o'clock, how- ever, a large number of. strangers had entered the chamber, having obtained tickets of admission from the Lord Cham- berlain's office. Upwards of 100 ladies obtained seats within the House itself—on the back Opposition benches— and there were also a large number of ladies in the strangers' gallery, to which on ordinary occasions only gentlemen are admitted. In the Ambassadors' gallery there were a large attendance of ladies and gentlemen. The opening ceremony commenced precisely at two o'clock, at which hour the Lord Chancellor, preceded by the Purse-bearer and the Sergeant-at-Arms (Lieutenant-Colonel Talbot) carrying the mace, entered the House from below the bar, and took his place on the woolsack. By this time there were between twenty and thirty peers in the House. The Lord Chancellor re-entered the House, attended by the other Lords Commissioners—namely, the Earl of Lethom. the Earl of Kintore, the Earl of Coventry, and Viecount Cross--a few minutes after two o'clock. The Com- missioners, who were attired in the scarlet and ermine robes of their rank, took their seats on a temporary bench placed in front of the throne, which, as is usual on such ormaeinns, was uncovered. The Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod (Sir James R. Drummond) was at once deepatched to request the attendance of the Speaker and the House of Commons to hear the Royal Commission read. Shortly afterwards the Speaker, attended by the Sergeant-at-Arms, the chaplain, and a large number of Commoners, made his appearance at the bar, and the nasal salutations were exchanged by him and the Royal Commissioners. The LORD CIIANCELLOa announced that as it was not convenient to her Majesty to be personally present, she had been pleaeed to caw° a Royal Commission tie he issued under the Great Seal in order that the preeent Parliament might be holden. At the request of his lordshie, the Read- ing Clerk (the Hon. Slingsby Bethel') read the Commission. After this the Lord Chancellor read the Speech from the Throne, in the followine• term. : THE QUEEN'S SPEECH.

_ MY LORDS AND GENTLEMEN,— My relations with all foreign Powers continue to be frienuly. The affairs of South-Eastern Europe are still in an un- settled condition, but I do not apprehend that any distur- bance of European peace will result from the unadjusted controversies which have arisen in that region. Whilst deploring the event which compelled Prince Alexander of Bulgaria to retire from the government of that Principality, I have not judged it expedient to interefere in the proceed- ings for the election of his successor until they arriee at a stage at which nay assent is required by the stipulations of the Treaty of Berlin. The task which has been undertaken by my Government in Egypt is not yet accomplished, but a substantial advance has been made towards the assurance of external and in- ternal tranquility. In Burmah operations have been conducted by my troops with bravery and skill for the purpose of extirpating the brigandage which has grown up during recent years of mis- government. The bands of marauders by whom Upper Burmah has been long infested are being dispensed, and many of the teacleraehave laid down their arms I enter- tain a confident hope that the general pacification of the country will be effected during the present season. Commercial treaties ere being concluded with the king- doms of Greece and Roumania. Papers on these subjects will be laid before you. GENTLEMEN OF TTIE HOUSE OF COMMONS,— The estimates for the ceming year will be submitted to you. They have been framed with a careful regard to econ- omy, and to the efficiency of the public service. MY LORDS AND GENTLEMEN: The condition of Ireland still requires your anxious atten- tion. Grave crimes have happily been rarer during the last few months than during a similar period in preceding years, but the relations between the owners and occupier; of land, which, in the early part of the autumn, exhibited signs of improvement, have since been serioueiy disturbed in some districts by organised attempts to entree the latter class to combine against the fulfilment of their legal obligations. The efforts of my Government to cope with this evil have been seriously impeded by difficulties incident to the method at present prescribed by statute for dealing with such offences. Your early attention will be called to Propesals for reform in legal procedure, which [WPM; necessary to secure the prompt and efficient administration to the criminal law. Since I last addressed you the Commissioners directed to inquire into certain subjects of great importance to the material welfare of Ireland have been actively prosecuting their labours. The report of the Commission on the opera- tion of the recent Act dealing with the tenure and purchase of land will be shortly laid before you, and will doubtless receive from you the early and careful attention which the serious importance of the subject demands. • Bills for the improvement of local government in Eng- land and Scotland will be laid before you, and, should cir- cumstances render it possible, they will be followed by a measure dealing with the same subject in Ireland. Bills for improving and cheapening the procees of private bill legislation in England, Scotland, and Ireland will be submitted to you. You will be asked to consider measures having for their object to remove hindrances which exist to the cheap and rapid transfer of the land, tee facilitate the pos- session of allotments for small householdlars, and to provide for the ready sale of glebe lands. The Commission which I issued in 1885 to inquire into the lamentable depression under evhich trade and agriculture' has been suffering for so many years presented a report, which, together with the important evidence collected by them, will shortly be laid before you. A Bill for altering the mode of levying tithes in England and Wales will be submitted to you. In regard to Scotland, you will be asked to •consider mea- sures of reform of the Universities for completing recent legislation, as to the powers of the Secretary for Scotland. and for amending the procedure of criminal courts. Measures dealing with the regulation of railway rates, and for preventinz fraudulent use of merchandise marks, will also be, brought under your consideration. In the performance of these and othn momentous duties I earnestly pray that the blessing of Almighty God may attend your labours. Lord SALISBURY, at the conclusion of the Speech, made a touching reference to the late Lord Iddesleigh whoee death, he said, had left an impression on his mind which he felt could never be effaced. His Lordship was one of the wisest and safest councillors the Q, Nett bad ever had, and was a man whose influence within the Cabinet and within his party was far higher and greater than was apparent to the public eye.—Earl GRANVILLE followed, and expressed the hope that the remembrance of Lord Iddeeleieh's qualities would have some effect in diminishing that bitterness of discussion which sometimes occurretat firms of political crises. The Addresein reply to the Sneech from the Throne was. moved by. the Earl/of ERNE.—Visconnt ToaurrreeroN se- conded the moticn.—Earl GRANVILLE, after a slight refer- ence to foreign affairs, expressed the hope that the Govern- ment would well consider their action in regard to Ireland. He pointed out that the question of local government in Ireland was relegated to a very uncertain period, and sub-. mitted that Her Maiesty's Government did not know hew to deal with tha administration of that country.---Lord SALIS- BURY, in referring to the resignation of Lord itan- dolph Churchill, said the other members of the Government did not differ from his Lordship in dissatisfaction at the public expenditure, but they differed from him as to the manner and time of expressing his views. He contended that the Irish policy of the Government could not be held to have failed before they had obtained and ap- plied special powers of enforcing the law. The noble Mar- gals added that nothing had occurred to give the Govern- ment the impression that the relations between France and Germany were otherwise than peaceful. The discussion in reference to Ireland was continued by Earl Spencer' Lord Ashbourne, Lord Herschell, and the Earl of Camperdown. The Address washagreed to before their lordships rose at eight o'clock. HOUSE OF COMMONS.—TIIURSDAY. - -

CHILDREN FolsomEn.—On Wednesday information Was furnished with regard to the death of two children named Wilkes at Hunt•street, Chiswick, apparently from poison. Four other children, members of the family, were placed under the care of medical men, suffering from what was diagnosed as irritant poisoning. EXTRAORDINARY CONFESSION OF WIFE MURDER.—it Manchester Police Court, on Tuesday, a man named James Bradbury was charged on his own Confession, with murder- ing his wife. The woman died a year ago, and at the in- quest a verdict of death from natural causes was returned. (in Monday the prisoner went to the detective office, sou gave himself into custody, stating that he killed his wife in ,a most horrible manner, and had not rested easily since. He was remanded for inquiries to be made. DEPUTATION OF FACTORY WORKERS.---A large deputation from the factory workers of Lancashire, Cheshire, and Der- byshire, waited on Thursday afternoon on the Home Secre- tary, and complained of the laxity with which the provi- sions of the Factory and Workshops Act are observed in a considerable number of factories in the northern part of the country. Children, young persons, and wcmen are be- ing worked beyond the specified hours, Sanitary and other regulations were being neglected, and in fact the Act threatened to become a dead letter. The deputation (who were accompanied by a large number of local members of Parliament) asked that a considerable addition should be made to the present staff of inspectors, due care being take,' to select persons who had a practical knowledge of machinery. MnMatthews promised to give the matter his earliest consideration.

In view of the number of members expected to hear Lord Randolph Churchill's statement, many gentlemen took time by the forelock on Thursday morning, and.came down early to secure seats, the first to arrive being as early as a quarter after eight. Members continued to arrive at intervals during the morning, a comparatively. large number having come down before eleven o'clock. Lord Rar.dolph Churchill arrived shortly before noon and secured the corner seat be. bind the Treasury Bench, the place occupied by Lord Har- tington during the tenure of office of Mr. Gladstone's last Administration. The corner seat on the second bench be. low the gangway on the Conservative side has been appro- priated by Mr. Chaplin. Nearly all the best seats bad been taken by noon, and members we then continuing' to arrive. A large crowd had assembled outside Palace Yard to witness the arrival of members.

PROCEDURE.—After the format business, the changes during the recess were announced by the SPEAKER, and new writs having been ordered for the scats vacant, Mr. W. H. SUITH intimated that he should at the earliest opportunity move resolutions relating to procedure of the House, and should ask the House to give the necessary facilities to pro- ceed with them from day to day, subject only to such in- terruption as might be necessary for the conduct of urgent public business.—After the Government notices of proposed legislation, an unusually large number of notices (amounting to nearly 200) were given by private members. LORD R. CHURCHILL'S RESIGNATION. Lord R. CHURCHILL made a statement bearing on his resiEnation of the office, of Chancellor of the Exchequer. The noble Lord stated that he resigned because he could net become responsible for the Estimates which were de- manded for the Army and Navy Departments. There were other matters on which he had the misfortune to differ with Lord Salisbury, matters perfectly capable of accomnaccla- tion ; but be was pledged to retrenchment and economy, and was convinced by his experience that each a Tolley could

Sir, —1 am desired by the Prince of Wales to acknowledge the receipt of a communicaticn signed by you on behalf of tl:v• "Isle of Man, Liverpool, and ManchestNr Steamship Co and to inform you in reply that his Royal Highness h.a, much pleasure in complying with your request for permis- sion to call one of the newly built steamers belonging to the company The Prince of Wales.—l have the honour to be, sir, your obedient servant, FRANCIS KNOLLYS. It wilt be remembered that, with the permission of her Majesty, the twin shin of the Prince of Wales has recently been moved Queen Victoria. It may be added that these two vessels. which are being rapidly pushed forward by one of the leid- ing firms on the Clyde, will be the fastest passenger bo its afloat. They will ply between Liverpool and the Isle of Man in the service of the Manx line.

Mr. J. F. Cheetham, formerly member for North Derbyshire, has offered £5OO towards the scheme for establishing a free library at Stalybridge, in celebration of the Queen's Jubilee. TORY LITTLENESS.—A well-known local Conservative at Cardiff has been caught defacing the statue of a local Liberal leader with yellow paint and tar. He was brought before the magistrates and bound over to appear again on Friday. The Hon. Mrs. Alister Campbell, who met with a serious accident last Thursday in the hunting field, near Chippenham, and has since been lying in a dangerous state from injuries to the spine at Harden Huish House, died on Monday. ROYAL VISIT TO BIRMINGHAM.— The Mayor of Bir- mingham has received intimation that the Queen will be pleased to lay the .foundation-stone of the new Law Courts, to be erected in Corporation-street. The date of the visit has not been fixed. HARD ON PAUPERS.—With a view of reducing the num- ber of able-bodied paupers in the workhouse, the Tam- worth Board of Guardians have decided to compel each Strong able-bodied man to break one ton of stone each dayeand those of less strength half a ton daily. The cloth making and tannery works of Messrs. Wm. and Henry Lister, at Dursley, took fire on Sunday, the flames originating in an oak bark rick of 300 tons, and spreading to the main building, which was still burning on Monday morning, and had been for 30 hours. The damage is great. Two MINF.RS CRUSHED TO DEATIT.—TWO men, named Henry Drabbler and Thomas Rosen, were killed on Mon- day morning whilst at work at the Pleasley Pit, near MLsfield. They were engaged in removing timber in one of the stalls, when a large fall of "bind" occurred, crushing the men to death. HEAVY SENTENCE FOR FORGERY.— At Leicestershire Assizes on Saturday, Frederick William Coleman, boiler- maker, of Loughborough, was indicted for forging a bill of exchange for £lO9 on Messrs. Jessops and Sons, iron- founders, of Leicester. He was found guilty, and sentenced by Mr. Justice Field to five years' penal 'servi- tude. Mr. Serjeant Sleigh died on Sunday at Ventnor, in his 86th year. The learned serjeant, who had been confined to his room for only a few days, never sat in Parliament, , though he had contested Frome, Lambeth, and Hudders- field in the Conservative interest. He was for many years the leading counsel for the Bank of England, and was ' well known in the civil as well as the criminal courts. How INFANTS ARE DISPOSED OF—At Wedriesbury, on Tuesday, Fanny Robinson, midwife, was charged with causing the death of the illegitimate child of Bridget Hines, of Darlaston. On Saturday, Hines gave birth to a male child, and was attended by the prisoner. Subse- quently the child was found dead. Its neck was broken, and the head was shockingly crushed. SHOCKING DEATH OF A FARMEL—PhiIip Berry, of Atherton, near Manchester, has met with a shocking death. He-was riding a pony on Leigh-road, and when passing under the railway arch at Chowbent Station the animal was startled by a passing train. It bolted and threw Berry, who alighted on his head, receiving such injuries that he died almost immediately. Deceased was well known and highly respected by the farmers in the 'district. He was 65 years of age. When the prosecutions com- menced there were 148 of these clubs in existence, the .Inajority of them being drinking dens of the worst description. At the present time there are not more ,than, 18. I A VETERAN Wannton.—There died a few days ago, at 13, Hester-street, Butler-street, Greenheys, John Pretty- johns, V.C., late colour sergeant in the Royal Marine Light Infantry, aged 62. The deceased, who was a native • of Plymouth, went through the Crimean War, and won , the following medals and honours :—Victoria Cross, for ivalour, battle of Inkerman, November 4, 1854; Victoria I Cross (miniature), presented by the officers of the i Plymouth Division R.M. to wear on undress occasions; • Crimean medal, three ba!rs (Sebastopol, Inkerman, and Balaclava); Turkish and Sardinian medals; China medal, one bar (Canton) ; gratuity, good conduct, and long ser- vice medals. I A LARGE SPANISH Co/41'1am. There is an im- mense contract for torpedo-boats and other warlike craft open in Spain. The Government of the Queen- Regent intends to spend no less than 0,000,000 for the purpose of placing the Spanish fleet on a proper footing. The money is to be raised by the sale of certain Crown lands. Naturally this is a proceas which requires time, and therefore a syndicate has been formed to finance these lands. We do not, profess to understand ' the nature of the operation or the whereabouts of the lands; but a correspondent states with some detail that ths syndicate has been completely successful, that the money required by the Government will be forth- -1 coming, and that the Chamber has passed the bill autho- rising the transaction. We hear that the agents of two ' or three Clyde ship-building firms are in Madrid making heroic efforts to secure this immense piece of business. A SENSATIONAL RANKRUPTCY.—Mr. George Chapman, ..of the firm of Chapman and Watts, drapers, Little [ Underbank, Stockport, was examined in the Stockport [Bankruptcy Court on Saturday. The debtor has been a Member of the Town Council for forty years. lie has filled the office of Mayor, and is now a magistrate. ansl. In the words of one of the questions put to him—which he answered in the affirmative—he has acquired "a repu- tation which induced people to trust him before death land after." He admitted that he had misappropriated [ money in “Bratt's estate," in lihich the people con- cerned were all infants. Their money had, he said, all gone. The bankrupt was examined in regard to other trust money which had disappeared, and also with refer- ence to his speculations on the Stock Exchange. His examination is not concluded. A great sensation has been caused in Stockport by Chapman's admissions. FATAL EXPERIMENT IN HANGING.—The Coroner for Westminster on Saturday received informatim of tho death of Vernon Edwards[lB, lately residing at a,Hunter- street, Brubswick-struare, who was found by a police- man banging in a stable in Park-lane, and who subse- quently died. Constable Puncher reports that on the afternoon of the 17th inst. he was informed that several boys had been playing, in a stable in Park-lane at hang- ing (one of them officiating as "Jack Ketch"),, and that an accident had occurred, the boy who was the last "subject" of the executioner being at the moment sus- pended by the neck from a strap arid probably dying, as all the other boys had gone away and left him to his fate. The constable at once ran to the spot, and found Edwards hanging as described, and almost black in the face. Puncher immediately cut the strap, and released the boy from his horrible situation. He was then neatly unconscious. Assistance was obtained, and he [was taken to St. George's Hospital; but he gradually sank, and expired.

EXTRAORDINARY 017TRAGE£4.—Extraordinary outrages on a widow (Mrs. Dutton) and her daughter are ieported from Chester. Mrs. and Miss Dutton occupy two cot- tages at Swanbach, Audlem, in which they have a life interest. They are Catholics and both declare that for some time they have been atrociously treated. Mrs. Dut- ton, who is 73 years old, states that her windows had been smashed, and her property damaged. A few days ago stones were thrown through her bedroom window ;she was in bed, and on getting up to look out was struck on the foreheadwith a stone, which inflicted a severe wound, from which she lost much blood. During another night someone discharged a gun at the cottages, shattering several slates on the roof. It has cost them considerable sums at varioui times.to repair the damages. Mrs. Dutton has appealed to the Home Secretary for pro- tection, who has sent a sympathetic reply. She has also been in communication with Cardinal Manning. Mrs: Dutton alleges that they are persecuted simply because they are Roman Catholics. DEATH OF SIR JOSEPH WHITWORTH, BART.—lntelli- gence was received in Manchester on Sunday night- of the death of Sir Joseph Whitworth, Bart. Sir Joseph's connection with Manchester had been a long and honour- able one, and extended so far back as the year 1818, ivhen he entered the factory of Messrs. Crighton, -and com- menced to study the construction of cotton machinery. After his marriage, in 1825, he went to London, but returned eight years later, and commenced business as a toolmaker. Thenceforward his rise was rapid, and his inventions, particularly of planing and measuring machines, attained world wide re- nown. Between the years 1850 and 1860 he was engaged perfecting his inventions in guns and projectiles. From the large fortune he acquired he set apart no less a sum than £lOO,OOO for the found- ation of the well-known Whitworth Scholarships in Science and Mechanical Construction, and was well aided by the Government, who added further exhibitions and grantedcapitation fees and sums of money for apparatuk The works erected by Sir Joseph Whitworth in the centre of Manchester grew unceasingly, and several years ago an entirely new establishment for the manu- facture of rifles, guns, projectiles, and heavy work of all kinds was erected at Openshaw, near Manchester. Sir Joseph resided for many years at the Firs, Fallowfield. and had a splendid estate in Derbyshire. He died at Monte Carlo on Saturday, aged 83. Sir Joseph Whitworth, Bart., F.R.S., was born at Stockport, in 1803. He had been a competitor with Sir W. G. Arm- strong in his efforts to produce ordnance for the national service that may combine every important requisite. He was created a baronet in October, 1869, in which year he instituted the "Whitworth Scholarships," consisting of thirty scholarships of £lOO a year each, tenable for two or three years, for the encouragement of mechanical and engineerrng science. Sir Joseph Whitworth was the author of "Miscellaneous Papers on Practical Subjects; Guns and Steel," 1873. The University of Edinburgh conferred on him the honorary degree of LL.D. in 1878. —The remains of the deceased will be removed from Monte Carlo to Stancliffe Hall, Rowsley, Derbyshire, the late residence of the deceased baronet, and interred in a vault at the Pariah Church, Dirley Dale, towards the end • of next week. k

THE ACTION AGAINST A PROTESTANTIk.
SISTERHOOD.

On Saturday, before Mr. Justice Kekewich, the further hearing of the case of Alcard v. Skinner Caine on. Miss Hannah Skinner, Lady Superior of the Protestant Con- meat of the Sisterhood of St. Mary of the Cross, in cross- examination by Sir Charles Russell for plaintiff, said that very large sums had been received from the sisters. attached to the convent\ and that the income in 18861 from funds invested was £11,718. Mr. fly. Daniel Nihill,, vicar of St. Michael's, Shoreditch, spiritual adviser tol the convent, said he recorded with his own hand eveaTi payment made in connection with the institution. never received any stipend from the convent at any, time, although he sometimes took his meals there. His; house was quite close to the convent building. .The books that had been produced contained entries of every( sum that had been brought into the sisterhood by the plaintiff. On Monday the Rev. Mr. Nihill, spiritual ad-, viser to the convent, was recalled, and said the+ ordinary expenses br carrying on the convent were defrayed out of contributions obtained by the sisters. This concluded the defendant's case, which the, Solicitor-General summed up. He contended that, in the first place, plaintiff had, by her own lachrs in notl bringing her action sooner, put herself out of court;', and, secondly, that the claim could not be justified, asi she had all along acquiesced in the mode in which the. money had been expended, namely, in the enlarging of.l the convent buildings. Sir Charles Russell on Tuesday addressed the' jury on behalf of Miss Allcard, the plaintiff. He, said that tbose who argued that in thisi case there was, a voluntary gift by the plaintiff to the defendant, must satisfy the court not thaethe pe7-4. son who made it understood merely what she was doing,i but that she should be safeguarded and protected leo what she did by competent independent legal advice.' He concluded by contending that the plaintiff had fully made out her case, and he asked, therefore, fora decreei forthe repayment of money advanced by the plaintiff to the defendant, with costs of the suit. His Lordship reserved judgment.

It will be of interest to the readers in this district to state that Miss Allcard is the daughter of Mr. William All-card, formerly of Bank House, Warrington, who many years ago unsuccessfully contested the borough against Sir Gilbert Greenell, who won by a majority of 27.

An Imperial decree was issued in Berlin prohibiting the export of horses from Germany. DEATH SENTENCE ON A FATHER —At Durham Assizes, on Tuesday, Thomas Thompson. 31, joiner, was sentenced to death for the murder of his son, a little boy, whose throat he cut. The accused had been out of work some time, and gave as his reason for commitOng the act that it wits better than their going into the workhouse. . .

FIVE Bcri's IcROWICED.—On Monday an inquest was held on the bodies of the five lads—named Atherton Pemberton, aged seven year,; Peter Priestley, aced seven; James Hall, aged nine Janice Murphy. aged 10; and James Webster, aged seven—who were on Friday drowned in pit on Cop. pull Moor, having ventured on the ice when it was unsafe in consequence of the thaw. A verdict was returned of "Accidentally drowned whilst sliding on the ice."

THE PHOSECI7TIOI.7 OF IRISH LEADERS - On Tuesday notices were served on Messrs. Dillon, William O'Brien, and Crilly. Informing them that the Crown will send thy bills against them for the Flair of Campaign conspiracy to the County Dublin Grand Jury, instead of the City at the ap- proaching Commission on thd Stb of February. The clarge against Mr. Matthew Harris, M.P., who is seriously ill, in Ballinasloe, has been abandoned for the present.

div.p: ence and those' who are directly or indirectly repre- sented at it are sincerely desirous of carrying agree- ment to the utmost possible limits, consistent with the maintenance of the principles which we may respectively consider fundamental." This being the Case, it Would seem that the difficulties are likely to vanish as they are re- solutely faced. This at any rate represents the position of Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, who again affirms that he has no objection to Home , Rule in the abstract. He wished, however, to limit it in Mr. GLADSToNB'S bill; and the' point to settle is whether a basis of limita- tion can be found to which all parties can agree. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN points to the relations which exist between the Dominion of Canada and the Canadian provinces; and quotes Mr. JUSTIN MCCARTHY, the vice- chairman of the Irish Parliamentary party, as having looked in a like direction. If Mr.' McCARTHY still holds to the views attributed to him, and if he at the same time fairly re- presents Irish opinion, it seems to us that a way out of the labyrinth may be readily found. But we are inclined to suspect that ' a good many things have happened since Mr. MCCARTHY suggested that Home Rule should be "based upon the establishment be- tween England and Ireland of similar rela- tions to those which exist between the provinces of Canada and Ottawa." There was a time, and it is not long since either, when the Irish leaders were disposed to lis- ten to proposals which did not go beyond, administration in local seligovernment. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN and Sir CHARLES DILKE had prepared to go to Ireland with a view to working on these lines; but meantime Lord RANDOLPH CHURCHILL, Or Lord CARNARVON, or botil combined, led the Nationalists to I believe that if they would put the Tories in office they would get a Parliament of their own. This was the making of history so far as the Irish Question was concerned; it caused Mr. GrAcisTon ta turn his attention to a scheme which should include legislation as well as administration, and as matters stood it Would appear that Ireland will now be content with nothing less. Mr. CHAM BERLAIN is disposed to have a fling at lush agitators, and he may be pardoned for "hit- ting back ; " but it becomes all sections of politicians to recognise that the voice of Ireland, constitutionally expressed under a widely extended suffrage, is loud in demand- ing that power shall be given the sister isle to make laws as well as administer them. A similar demand has been made on behalf of Scotland and Wales; and for our part, as we have repeatedly stated, we do not see why there should not be four minor Home Rule Parliaments, one for each country, with an Imperial Parliament with representatives from each country, to deal with Im- perial affairs. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN is mov- ing on, and moving on in this direction; but Lord HARTINGToN is a long way behind, if the opinions which he expressed in his ad- dress to the electors of the Rossendale Division (from which Mr. CHAMBERLAIN quotes) are to be taken as his maximum of concession. We would fain hope that he, too, is advanc- ing, for, whatever may be agreed upon, the Liberal party cannot be said to be either completely or satisfactorily united until not only the member for West Birmingham, but the member for Rossendale, has re- turned to the fold. Lord HARTINGTCN is to sneak on Wednesday next at Newcastle- on- Tyne, and we may be quite sure that at this juncture he will weigh his words with more than ordinary care. He is the leader of the Unionist party, and he is, moreover, pledged to support the present Government in certain eventualities. His lordship is not the man either to lightly give or lightly break his word, and, making a forecast, we should be disposed to say that he will stand where lie is for a time. It may be, indeed, that Lord HARTINGTON will leave it to the logic of events to settle certain things for him ; he does not share Mr. CHAMBERLAIN'S advanced views on the Irish Land Question, for he is not a pioneer of progress ; but we are in- clined to think he will come in after the death —the death of the SALISBURY Government.

THE rumours as to impending war in Europe are on the increase, and if we are to believe some of our contemporaries, the out- break of hostilities is in ail likelihood a mat- ter not of months, but of days. All this may be true; but it certainly ought not to be true. There is nothing like an adequate cause for war—look where we will. A few months ago the talk was as to the possibility of Aus- tria and Russia flying at each other's throats; and the fear was that England, from her in- terest in the Bulgarian question, might be drawn into the conflict. Prince BISMARCK was reported to be holding himself aloof, and not at all likely to be distressed, whoever weakened themselves by fighting, so long as Germany kept out of it. Now we hear of the possibility of immediate war between France and Germany, and there are some signs undoubtedly which point in that direc- tion. The German CHANCELLOR has dis- solved Parliament because it will not grant him complete control of the army for seven years at a stretch; but the significant thing is that he did not hesitate to say that he wanted a larger army and larger powers, b cause he believed that sooner or later Germany would, be at war with France. He wants to be ready for the struggle, and when it comes, to use his own brutal words, to be in a position to " bleed France white." Language of this kind is calculated to provoke that feeling of hatred which sometimes leads to war, and it may be that this is Prince BISMARCK'S ob- ject. The Germans are understood to be better equipped than the French, being well supplied with repeating rifles, whilst the French troops are furnished with the carbine. The German Government are reported to have made provision with a London firm for supplying the German army with preserved meats ; a prChibition has been issued against the exportation of horses ; and the people of Metz have been warned that women and children may be called upon to remove from the place at short notice. France, on the other hand, is now making a move in the direction of the frontier, arrangements being made for erecting huts for the troops. Ger- many is reported to be so disturbed by this counter-stroke that it is said an explanation will be demanded, which may be followed by an ultimatum, if the reply received is not regarded as satisfactory. It would seem in- credible that there should be this " Much ado about nothing," if we did not know from past experience that the madness of " monarchs and statesmen " is never more cledrly revealed than in the causes assigned for going to war. That France has during the last dozen 3 ears repeatedly shown herself bitter against Germany, on account of the loss of Alsace and Lorraine, has been obvious to the whole world ; but that surely does not justifiy Prince BISMARCK in speaking of what he will do when he gets the opportunity of outting his foot on the neck of the enemy. he made a great mistake when he annexed Alsace and Lorraine; for, although years

div.head: EXAMIgRft. SATURDAY, JANUARY 29. 1887.
div.p: THE EXAMIgRft. SATURDAY, JANUARY 29. 1887.

have elapsed since this vicious transfer took place, the people in these provinces are still French in habit and sentiment, and were spoken of by the German CHANCELLOR himself, no later than Monday last, as irreconcilable. Ah ! if Germany could only rise to the occasion,and say—" These people are not with us, or of us ; let them be united again to the country of their choice "—how much better it would be than plunging into a war in which millions of property may be de- stroyed, and tens of thousands of men slaugh- tered! What does it profit Germany to hold a strip of country which forces her to keep a standing army, the burden of which is weigh- ing her down, and which, at the same time, compels France, terribly to her injury, to follow suit? All that is really needed is the exercise of the elementary principles of jus- tice, and this would be done if the people of each country would assert themselves the more with a view to checking usurpation of authority on the part of their rulers. It is satisfactory to recognise that the people of Germany are not disposed to be "ordered about" as they have been : and that there are limits even to the power of "the man of blood and iron." In this country, too, there is a growing disposition to seek to control the treaty-making powers of the Crown ; and this means that the masses perceive that a policy of non-intervention in affairs that do not closely concern us is allied to the righteousness which exalteth a nation. Let U 3 hope that the war cloud which seems to be settling over France and Germany will pass away and leave both coun- tries to live and thrive in the sunshine of 11 prosperity.

There is an English Home Ruler at St. Helens who wants ruling both at home and abroad. He has been brought before the maristrates for abusing the Town Clerk in the streets ; and, ai he used, language of the most abominable kind, he may consider that he has been leniently treated in being simply bound over to keep the peace. He was in the habit, he said, of " makiug furl for the people," but if he cannot be funny in a less outrageous way it will become necessary to put him in a strait jacket—or in gaol.

The Warrington Liberal Club looked quite gay at the re-opening which was held on Monday evening, after alteration, decoration, ventilation, and general "botheration" which always attends renovazion. There was a feed of course—no Englisman can be expected to rejoice until he has used a knife and fork— and later on there was a ••judicious mixture" of speeches and billiards. The announce- ment that the club was free from debt gave great satisfaction, and it is not less satisfac- tory to be able to state that Liberal-Union- ists have contributed just as liberally with that object as other Liberals.

Mr. W. Unsworth, who, from the descrip- tion which he gave of himself at the town's meeting at Warrington the other 'night, would seem to be a sort of exhibition agent. says he gave way to the library scheme taking -priority "with a distinct understanding that if they were allowed to introduvi their sub- ject first they would support the exhibition scheme." This is absolutely untrue; he gave way because he knew that, if he did not, the question of freeing the library might come against him as an amendinent, and that he would be bowled out with the first ball. Mr. Unswortli is evidently good at drawing the long bow, and he may be 'good at climbing the greasy pole; but as to that we shall see —when the exhibition comes off.

RUNCORN 2ND STARR BOWHETT BUILDISO SOCIFTY.— In connection with this society an anoropriation meeting was held in the office of the secretary (Mr. W. Handley) on Thursday evening. Mt. George Moss presided. Mr. S. Pope drew attention to a pamphlet which had been issued in the town instituting an unfair comparison between an all-ballot society, such as theirs, and a ballot and sale so. cietv, and a conversation ensued in vindication of the prin- ciples of Starr Bowkett Building Societies. By a calcula- tion, which Mr. Handley declared to be incontrovert- ible it was shown that, putting matters in tbe worst light for the Starr Bowkett Society, an annropriation of £3OO, bought at a premium of £3O 5s per £lOO, as fixed by the pamphlet, would he £33 138 cheansr in the end than in the Ballot and Sale Society. The Chairman pointed out that as a matter of practice their half appromia- Cons were sold at a premium of £8 per £lOO ; and asked if the system of ballot was so had as the Pamphlet would have them to believe. Why did not the society that issued it do away with that branch of their business. Mr. Firth referred to a clause in the pamph- let, which asked if it was to the interest of working-men to join a Society Out of which he could not get a halfpenny if at death's door, or if his wife and family were starving. Mr. Handley said-there was nothing in the rules of the ballot and tale society that would permit even themselves to do this. In the Starr-Bowkett Societies inßuncorn the widows of deceased members in numerous instances had had the subscriptions paid In fall, without any deduction for expenses. Those present expressed their confidence in the Starr-Bowkett system. Sebsequently an appropriation took place and resulted in Mr. John Green, Plasterer, Portland- street, who had only joined the society that evening, being entitled to £2OO, free of interest for 12f, years.

He acknow- ledged that he had done that without the consent of the plaintiff.—Hls Honour told the defendant he was Very fool- ish to defend a case on those grounds, and he most pay the money At the rate of Ll a month. CLAIM FOR Weems. &c.—An action was brought by Thomas Hoggarth, living in a cottage at House Farm,Nor- ton, against E. M. Woodward, farmer, of Howe Farm, Nor. ton, for £5O. The claim was originally for £5l 12s 63, but the plaintiff abandoned the £l. 123 ed In order to bring the case within he jurisdiction of the county court. The plaintiff's claim was made up of wages due, £26 for wrong- ful dismissal, and money advanced to permit the defend- ant's wife to take butter to Warrington, items for harm, bread, and porridge for dogs.—Mr. Seger, barrister (instruc- ted by Mr. John Ashton) appeared for the praintiff, and Mr. Worthington, solicitor, Manchester, represented the defen- dant. The case occupied the attention of the court .from eleven o'clock in the morning until nearly five o'clock In the evening, and had than to be adjourned for a month be- cause the evidence hail been concluded. It appeared that the plaintiff had been second herdsman to Lord Bective, an Westotureland, and whilst there he saw an advertisement in a newspaper, and he answered it, and subeequentlY had an inmrview with the defendant, and his father-in-law, Mr. Knowle3, farmer. The result was defendant engaged the plaintiff as dairyman at 26s per week, with milk, vegetables, and cottage free. Another interview afterwards took place at Kendal. and the defendart said "I must have a tie on vpn. I will keep a share of his wages, Si) that it von leave me within twelve months you will not get that. Plaintiff said all right; it's as fair for one as for the other. If you turn me away lr,fore the time has expired you must pay up. He came to Norton on March 20th, 1886, end his family came the followine month Mary Hoggarth, plain- tiff's wife, and Kate Jones. of Gilbert-street, Runcorn, f.'n, merly employed at the defendant's house, gave evidence in favour of the terms of the agreement described. Mrs. Hog- garth also proved several items for dog porridge, colouring for butter, So.—Edward Rawlinson, gardener, Norton, de- posed to the plaintiff feeding the dogs with porridge, com- posed of meal, bran, and flour. —William Speakman, engine- man, employed by Sir Richard Brooke, stated that to feed the cattle the plaintiff was only allowed a bag of oats a week, but his inccessor married Gib,on, had five pr six bags a week. -- The first sitting of the new County Court for Widnes was held on Thursday, under favouiable auspices. There was a fair amount of business, but that was a matter of course ; a County Court for the Widnes district has been needed for some time.

The Mayor of Warrington (Dr. Mackie) having resigned in consequence of his pro- longed illness, it will be for the Town Council to elect a successor. Who will take the post? It seems to be taken for granted that the Jubilee Mayor must be a gentleman with a full purse and a free hand.

The Deputy Mayor caving reported to the General Purposes Committee the result of the Town's Meeting on the question of celebrat- ing the Queen's Jubilee, it is understood that the matter will come before the Town Coun- cil at its meeting on Tuesday next. It may be, however, that the Jubilee question will be left over until after the election of a new Mayor, for which purpose there will probably be a special meeting of the Council.

The Secretary of the Scottish Home Rule Association is looking ahead ; and he urges Welshmen to look ahead also. The best hone, he says, for Scotland and Wales lies in a general measure of national self-government alike granted to all the four nationalities, who can, as at present, unite in an Imperial Par- liament for Imperial affairs. "And so say all , of us."

Patrick Bryson, an inmate of the Prescot Workhouse, has been having a little discus- sion with another inmate; and in the course of it he enforced his argument with a pocket knife. It is stated that Patrick isn't quite " sharp;" but it seems the knife was, for it went through the upper lip of his opponent. It is understood that the argument will be resumed, in a more rational way, at the Liver- pool Assizes.

The Deputy-Mayor of Warrington, in pre- siding at St. Paul's taa party. expressed his rearet at the absence of Sir Gilbert Greenall, because, he said, he would have "contribu- ted as much as possible to their amusement." Just so; he is, to quote his own description of himself, "an odd old fellow." He is what the Yankees call "an amusing cuss '' ; for nobody regards him as a serious politician. And yet it is serious, in these stirring times, to be represented by such a politician.

Having gone over to the Tories, Mr. Goschen would seem anxious to "let the dead past bury its dead." " Union, Union, for ever," was his cry on Monday night. Nice man, truly, to talk about union who has been the cause, for a dozen years, of disunion in the Liberal party. He has been what Mr. Chamberlain called him, the " Skeleton of the Feast ;" and the guests breathe more freely now that he has taken himself away.

Oh, but Mr. Goschen says :—" I stand here as the champion of my country. I at least am not going to libel her past or imperil her future." A fine champion of his country certainly, when he struggled against the ex- tension of the franchise to the very men whose suffrages he has been seeking, and again placed himself in opposition when it was I sought to give votes to his fellow-countrymen 1 in the counties. He treated them as unfit for the franchise ; but the electors are avenged—they have treated him as unfit to be their representative, --- Mr. Goschen tries to found an argument against Home Rule in the fact that " the Americans did not allow separation in their own case, but staked their national exist- ence, staked their prosperity for many years to come, upon a death struggle rather than disintegrate a rising nationality." But the cases are not analogous. The Southern States when they sought separation possessed Home Rule; and they took up arms against the mother country—the Federal Union. Give Ireland such a legislature of her own as each of the Southern States possessed, and they will be content; there will be no talk about separation.

But we musn't be hard on the man who, although he is a tremendous personage in the Ministry, hasn't as much as a seat in the House of Commons. What a pity it is Tory officials couldn't count him in ! They tried •hard. It was Mr. Goschen who refused to give the Tories a blank cheque; but as things go they will begin to think that he has chinged his mind—that in offering himself he becomes a check or another kind. But never mind ; let the fireworks flare ; sound the trumpet and beat the drum, even when the conquering hero doesn't come.

Martin Dooley, of St. Helens, has been made to realise under disagreeable circum- stances that fast bind means fast find. He became surety for the good behaviour of his friend Patrick Macnamara ; but Patrick could not behave well for three months even, and the result is that Martin has been called upon to meet the bond of £5 into which he entered, as he said, "for the sake ot humanity." "Men should be what they seem ;" but, alas, neither men nor things are %at all times what they seem.

How BREAD IS CHEAPENED AT WIDEES.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, William Rudd was charged with selling bread without weighing it.—P C. Almond on the 22nd inst. went into the defendant's shop in Waterloo- road, and asked for a 41b loaf of bread. He was supplied by an assistant, who did not weigh the loaf. Ile remarked, "We don't weigh 31. loaves." The defendant was notla the shop.—The defendant said his orders were to weigh every loaf. The constable was told the loaf did not weigh 4lbs, but it was good weight for the money.—A fine of 103 and costs was imposed. Lactossn.-- Widnes v Liverpool (2.)—Played at Waver- tree, On Saturday, resulting in a victory for Widnes by three goals to two. Neither side was fully represented, Widnes being without Gosiage and Longton. The Widnes attacks led off at a great pace; scoring in the first five min- utes. At half-time Widnes led by two to one, and, although the Liverpool men played up better in the second half, the visitors always kept ahead, finally winning as above stated. Forster on the defence, and Wylde on the attack, played really well, notwithstanding the fact that they hail not had a game for six weeks. Baker and Slott defended well for Liverpool, bet were beaten by the superior speed of the Widnes attacks.

, Format. OF Mac Huottns.—The mortal rerrigins of Mrs. Jane Hughes, formerly of Saberlanthstreet, Runcorn, were interred on Monday afternoon at the Parish Churn!), Run- corn. The deceased, who was the widow of Samuel Hughes, at one time a captain of one of the Bridgewater steamers, was born on the 25th January, 1791. Had she lived until Tuesday last she would consequently have attained her 96th year. Mrs. Hughes for more than 70 years had been a member of the Wesleyan Society in Run- corn, and by her fellow members she was highly respected for her Christian character. At ninety years of age the deceased was able to read her Bible without the aid of spec- tacles, but during the last two or three years she was quite blind. • Her feneral was attended by several members of the Wesleyan body, and the burial service was conducted by the Revs. George Wood and A. P. Watson. The tables were pre- sided over by Mrs. Wylde, Mrs. Jones. Mra. Ackerley, Mrs. A. Povey, Mrs. J. M. Baguley. Mrs. Joseph Stokes. the Misses Johnstone, Miss Chrimes, Miss Short, Mies Piekop, Miss Rutter, and Miss Tickle. Subsequently the usual entertainment took place. The chair was taken by the Rey. John Lockwood, who was supported by Mr. Chnrchwarden Stokes.—The Chairman said tbar on the whole the past ear might be considered to have been a very happy one for the perish. Their congregation had in- creased, and, what was of still greater importance, was the fact that the number of their communicants had also in- creased. At Christmas aid at the new year they had 100 c'ommunicants, whichihe thoeht was a sure test of church. manship. Their day schoole had obtained first-class reports from her• Majesty's Inspector, and the grant earned was a very substantial amount. He was glad that their educa- tional institutions were in so prosperous a state, and that they still remained under the same tianagement.—A varied programme was then gone. through, and the proceedings cloeed with the usual votes of thanks. FATAL' RAILWAY ACCIDENT AT WIDNEA.—On Tuesday, before Mr, Clarke Aspirin'', coroner of Liverpool, an inquest was held on the body of Bernard Healey, 28 years of age, a labourer in the employ of the London and North-Westorn Railway Company, who resided with his bsother at 'Union Bank Cottages, Bold. It would appear that a man named James Naylor relieved the deceased as a watchman at a bridge in course of erection at Vineyard Crossing, near Wid- nes. The deceased was the watchman lor the day,aancl Naylor for the night. The deceased was relieved shortly after seven o'clock. It was dark, but not foggy. He went along the line towards Appleton, walking in the six foot: Soon afterwards Naylor heard that Healey had been knocked down near Appleton Station. A passenger train from Ditton to St. Helens had passed shortly after the de- ceased had 'Mt his post at the new bridge. The deceased had no lamp with him—'David Pairclough, a fi'reman, stated that he was with a coal train from Wigan to Garton. At Appleton 'Station the driver of the passenger train already referred to told him that he thought he had knocked some one dovn. Speed was slackened on the coal train, and about 400 yards from the station the deceased was found lying on his face in the four-foot of the up line. From Vineyard, signal-box a message was sent to Widnes for as- sistance, and an engine was sent for him. Fairclough was with'him until the arrival of the engine. The deceased was quite insensible.—Henry Meadows, the driver of the passenger train, said that be was going about 15 miles an hour between Vineyard Crossing and .A.ppleton, and for about two seconds heard a 'noise about the engine wheels, but saw • nothing. He thought, nevertheless that something was run over, and reported it at Appleton.—Atichard Hitchmough, a foreman shunter, stated that a doctor saw the deceashd Widnes, after . which he was brought to Lime-street by a special engine. Death ensued On Sunday , morning at six o'clock.—Verdict, "Accidental death."
