CONSECRATION OF Sr. PAUL'S CHURCH, WIDNES. The Church of St. Paul, Widnes, was formally conse- crated for public worship on Tuesday afternoon last. For upwards of two years. however, divine service has been celebrated in the sacred edifice, and crowded congregations have been attracted on nearly every Sabbath. After the erection of the building the one obstacle to consecration was the want of a houndary wall, as without " God's acre " is thus encircled Bishop Rvle has a conscientious objection to perform the formal ceremony of dedication. This difficulty was soon removed. Mr. T. S. Timinis, J.P., who had con- tributed the handsome sum of npoo to the Church Exten- sion Scheme, generously undertook to defray the cost of the wall, which amounted to nearly £BOO. The church has been previously described at length in this journal, but it may be interesting to repeat that it stands within an acre of ground, given by Mrs. Gerard Legh. Built from the de- signs of Mr. EL Shelmerdine, architect, of Liverpool, the edifice is cruciform in shape, and constructed in the early English style of architecture. It occupies a prominent posi- tion in Widnes-road, and is in the exterior and in the inte- rior a handsome building. The material principally used in its construction is grey pressed brick, but it is profusely decorated with terra-cotta, which best resists the Widnes atmosphere, and the roof is of red tiles. The seats, which are formed of pitch pine, varnished, are free and unappro- priated, and provide accommodation for 750 wor- shippers. The cost of the church was £B,OOO. Although the consecration service was held in the after- noon, the church was well filled with a congregation that thoroughly entered into the service. The Lord Bishop of the Diocese nok a position within the communion, and the clergy present in the chancel were the Rev. Canon LefroY (archdeacon el Warrington), Rev. T. Chambers (rector of Halewood), Rev. J. Wright-Williams (vicar of Widnes), Rev. W. Preston (vicar of llo'y Trinite, Runcorn), Rev. S. A. Spooner (St. Ambrose, Whines), Ray. J. Stowell, Hey. James E Lawton (curate, Farnworth), and Rev. A. P. Hamilton Wilson and Rev. J. R. Jones (curates, Widnes). The Bishop's secretary, at the outset, read the petition to his Lordship asking that the church should be consecrated, and the petition was supported by the personal presence in the chancel of the following laymen :—Messrs. T. S. Tirnmis, J P., John Brock, JP., G. Pilkington, J.P., and H. Wade Deacon; and Messrs. F. Neil and L. Kilcroes, churchwardens. The bishop and clergy then walked in procession round the church, repeating the 24th Pealm, and subsequently the bishop off ered up several special prarere for the occasion. The ceremony concluded with the reading of the bishop's senteece of consecration. Evening service was now cele- brated. The prayers were said by the Rev. A. P. Hamilton Wilson and the Rev. J. R. Jones, and the Rev. T. Cham- bers read the first lesson, an i Archdeacon Lefroy the second lesson. The Bishop delivered a discourse based on the 15th, 16.1), and 17th verses of the 11th chapter of St. Mark. He , pitied the person, he said, whose heart did not feel a deep I interest iu an occasion like that. They were setting apart for the service of Alinighty God 3 building which would stand long after they were dead. Who could tell what good the services and the preaching might do, and what an I awakening and convincing and conversion of souls might take place within that building. He had always felt a great interest in the Church life of Widnes. When through the providence of God he became Bishop of Liverpool, one of the first places in the diocese he passed through was Widnes. When he passed over that wonderful bridge that spanned , the Mersey, and looked upon the countless chimneys and the humble dwellings, he could not help thinking what I might be the spiritual condition of the people gathered in the place. When he found that there was only one little church for Widnes his heart was moved with pity, and he felt the deep necessity that a change should take place for the better. He thanked God that since he became bishop this church of St. Paul was the second he had consecrated, anel he believed that in that diocese the Church of England would yet raise its head higher and higher than ever she : had done before. Alluding to his text, his lordship said the first lesson to be learned was to reverence any place where the worship of God was carried on, and he urged that the service of the Church of England, one of the most democra- tic there was, should net be one of mere outward observance ) in which the preacher and the choir took the principal part, , but should be joined in by the whole congregation with the heart and soul.—During the service the choir sang an L anthem. A collection was taken in aid of the fund for erecting a parochial room in connection with the church. In the evenieg a service was held, when the Rev. Canon Eyre, M.A., vicar of St. Helens, preached to a good congregation. Services have also been held on each sac- ' needing evening, and the pulpit has been occupied by the • Rev. J. H. lioneyburne, M.A., vicar of St. Philemon's, Liverpool; Rev. T. Oliver, D.D., vicar of Garston ; and the b Rev. J. P. Cushing, of St. John's, Liverpool. On Sunday, ; the vicar, the Rev. J. Wright-Williams, will prea.eh morning ) and evening.

WIDNES COUNTY COURT. YESTERDAY.—Before his Honour Judge T. P. E. Thompson. WELCOME TO HIS HONOUR. The first sitting of the Widnes County Court was held yesterday. Upon his Honodr taking his seat, Mr. W. T. Husband said a deputation of Widnes tradesmen had waited upon him, and asked him on their behalf—and he did so on his own behalf—to express their very great obligations to his Honour for fixing 12 sittings a year in Widnes, thus meeting the wants as well as the wishes of the local - people. He did not know how it affected the bar of St. Helens. They were there that day to speak for themselves. It was his wish, and the wish of all inter- ested that his Honour might be long spared to administer justice in Widnes in the conscientious manner that he had done at St. Helens and Liverpool. The attendancs of his Honour, of the registrar, and the high bailiff WAS looked. upon as quite an event in the annals of Widnes.—Mr. H. L. Riley, of St. Helens, joinekin Mr. Husband's good wishes to his Honeur.—His Honour said he was much obliged to them for their good wishes. and added that they started tinder very good auspices, for that was as tine a day as they had had for a long time. TRAP ACCIDENT.—CLAIM FOR DAMAGES. John Smith, keeper of the Griffin Inn, Farnworth, brovght an action against Alfred Parkes, landlord of the Central Hotel, Widnes, to recover £2 lOs 4d, for damages caused to the plaintiff's trap, by a collision with another trap driven by the defendant's eervant.—The plaintiff was represented by Mr. C. H. Lewin, and Mr. W. 1. Husband was for the defendant. —lk.appeared from the opening state. of Mr. Lewin, that on the 10th August last the plaintiff, accompanied by his wife and a son, was driving frqm Fan- worth to Widnes. A. trap belonging to the defendant was . following in the same direction, 150 yards behind. Having had to pall up to prevent running over a flock of geese, the defendant's trap got within 10 yards of the plaintiff's con- veyance. He started again, but had almost immediately to pull up to prevent running over a child, when the defend- ant's trap dashed into his gig behind, overturning and smashing the gig, whilst the occupants were thrown out. Mr. Parkes had made an offer of 103 to settle, buf this was, of course, refused.—The plaintiff, his wife and son, gave testimony corroborating there facts. Samuel Francis, fishmonger, Albert-road, and William Streets, wheelwright, Albert-road, also gave evidence.—For the defence Mr. Husband submitted that the collision was a perfect accident, which would not have occurred had not Mr. Smith pulled up suddenly he save a child's life.— Samuel Whitfield, cow keeper, was called, but admitted that he had not seen the alision.—James Williams, but- cher, said the driver for the defendant did all in his power to prevent a collision.—Tbemas Campbell, the driver of the defendant's trap, corroborated.—ln reply to Mr. Lewin, he said the horse he was driving was a very hard mouthed animal, and he could not pull it up after the codision had occurred for a considerable distance.—lts Honour consi- dered the defendant liable. As to the contentioa that the plaintiff did not give warning that he was about to pull up, had he occupied his hands and mind in doing so, the child would have been run over. Judgment WAS entered for the plaintiff with costs.

THEFT OF PIGEONS: BADGERING A WITNESS.—Ezra Ver- non (15), son of a railway signalman, was charged with stealing three pigeons at Acton Grange. value 3s, the pro- perty of a market gardener named William Massey, on the 15th inst.—Prosecutor stated that he missed three of his pigeons on the 17th inst. Information was given to the police, who found the pigeons at a Mrs. Woodhouse's. at Daresbary.—Sarah Ann Woodhouse, a married woman, i stated that her husband was in the habit of buying pigeons. She bought three from the prisoner, who said they were his property, and gave him 26 3d for them. She could not identify the pigeons produced as being those she purchased from the prisoner.—The Magistrates' Clerk (Mr. Nichol. son): Do you buy pigeons without looking at them ?.—Wit- ness : I simply looked at them, and I cannot tell whether these are the pigeons I purchased.—The Chairman warned her that she would get herself into a serious difficulty if she did not mind.—Witness still gave the same answer, and Mr. Nicholson, addressing her, said, "Do you mean to tell the magistrates that von did not look at them ?"—Witnees : I did not notice them.—The question was repeated, and witness replied, •• I didn't take Chem into my hands to look at them."—The Magistrates' Clerk : Did you look at them? —Witness still give an unsatisfactory reply, and was pro- ceeding to make a rambling statement, when the Chairman informed her that she was not speaking the truth.—Witness: Begging your pardon. I sin—The Chairman : Do you ex- pect us to believe that you buy things without looking at them ? Did you look at the pigeons before buying them ? —Witness : I did not. tam certain I did not.—ln reply to Mr. Long, she said her husband was in the habit of buying pigeons.—The Chairman : Do you buy them without look. log at them ?—VVitness repeated that she did not take them into her hands —The Chairman : Yes or no P—Witness : I
did not.—The Chairman : You want us to believe that 7

Witness It is it:ue:::-A-fl.neo-f-10-8-;nd-oc-*;t;,OL: a fortnight's imprisonment, NVA9 imposed.—Mrs. Woodhouse was ordered to stand forward, and the Chairman, addressing her, said the Bench were very much dissatisfied with the way she had given her evidence. She would, therefore, have no ex- penses allowed her for her attendance as witness. He might perhaps warn her that an action could be taken against her fo. buying stoles property.—Mrs. Woodhouse (interrupt- ing) : I didn't know.—The Cuairman informed her that if she appeared before the Court in a similar case she might be prosecuted, and the consequences would be very severe.

FRIGHTFUL WIFK MURDER—Thomas Bloxham, aged 61, was charged at Leicester Assizes on Tuesday with the wil- ful murder of his wife, Ann Bloxf,am, at Leicester. The prisoner was jealous of his wife, who, he alleged, had com- mitted bigamy twice. He procured a pistol and shot her through the head, and afterwards stabbed her through the heart, and almost cut the head from the body. The prisoner said he and the deceased had agreed to commit suicide. He was found guilty and sentenced to death,

SANKEY RANGERS -Y.-W-A-R-RI-N-G-T-07N-OLYMPIC.—PIayed on the ground of the latter on Saturday, and resulted in a draw in favour of the Rangers. Score :—Sankey Rangers, 1 try 4 minors, to 1 try 2 minors. WARRINGTON GRA3IMAR SCHOOL v. CHORLTON "A" TEAM.—The Grammar School began the second part of the season by defeating the Chorlton team by one goal and 5 minors to 2 tries and 3 minors. Both teams played a fast and exciting game, and there was little to choose between the two.

SUTTON FREE WANDERERS V. STAR OF HOPE (WARRING. TON.)—These clubs met on the grosnd of the latter, on Saturday last, and a good game was played, the result being a victory for the home team. The score at the call of time was—Warrington, 1 drop goal and 4 minors, to Sutton 1 try (disputed) and 3 minors. Feruswoarn v. Lowe HOUSE TRUE BLUE.—These teams met at St. Helene, on Saturday, to play thair return match, and after a pleasant and well-contested game, the result was a victory far Farnwortb by 1 goal and 6 minors to nil. Farnworth journeyed with eleven men, but managed to pick up two Babe, thus playing with 13 men. RUNCORN (15) v. LIVERPOOL DISTRICT (17.)—Played at Runcorn on Saturday. This match WAS arranged by the Committee of the Runcorn Football Club, as a benefit match to assist a member of the Montrose Football Club, who unfortunately got his leg broken during the Junior Cup competiti. us. A good game resulted in a win for the home players, who scored one goal two tries and eight minors, to one goal one minor. H. Andrews obtained the two tries, H. Speakman being successful in dropping a goal from the field. McGeachin got the try for the District team. Cawley and Davies played a capital threequarter game, the forwards playing with their accustomed vigour. Amongst the District players. McGeachin end Woodward behind. and Wilcock, Raisbeck, and Dodd forward, were very conspicuous. The fund will be most substantially augmented by the "gate.". .

Wipszs V. Btneft.—These teams met at Birch on Satur- day, when a fast aud well-cantested game resulted in a vic- tory for the visitors by one goal, two tries. and five minors to three minors. Play during the first half was very even, each team scoring two minors; but in the second half, when they had the advantage of the slope, Whines corn- pletely out-played their opponents, Howard, Farrell, and Ridyard gaining tries by sterling play. Harding was also near scoring, being knocked in touch after running half the length of t' e field. Morris landed a beautiful goal. Hughes played a splendid game throughout. He was by far the best forward on the field, and was ably supported by Kiddie, Smith, Wood, and Ridyard ; whilst behind the pack Far- rell, Howard, Harding, and Bingham did good work. Thorn. ley and Allan were the pick of the home team. Teams : Widnes: S. Bingham, back ; Harding, Morris, and Pen- nington, three-quarter backs • Farrell and Howard, half backs ; Kiddie (captain), Smith, Ridyard, Wood, Pervin, Hughes, J. Bingham, Fogg. and Hardman, forwards. Birch: Pymm, back; Allan, T. Higginbottom, and Wheeler, throe-quarter backs; E. Higginbottorn and Holdsworth, half backs ; Thernley, Rigby, W. Higginbottom, Ferr- man, Beck, Cheetwood, Frost, Harrop, and Jackson, for- wards.

WARGLINGTON SECOND v. SANZET FIRST.—The return match between the above teams took place on Saturday afternoon, on the ground of the latter, before a goodly num- ber of spectators. Sankey were well represented, but the Warrington team were without the services of Coyne and Howarth. Bate won the toss. Ashton started the sphere, which dropped in touch, and the Warrington captain called the ball back. Ashton again kicked off and Bibby returned to centre, and after a good bit of passing, Mather secured a try for the visitors, Davies failing at goal. Barton dropped out, and after a bad pees by Boyle Myles secured a try, the kick at goal failing. Half time arrived with the score one try each. Recornmencing,Bate kicked off, ands poor return being made a scrimmage was formed in the home team's twenty-five. From a loose scrimmage Bate secured another try for the visitors, his attempt at goal failing. The War- rington team, not to be denied, again invaded the home twenty-five. The play during this half on behalf of both teams was good, but the visitors' forwards carried scrimmage after scrimmage with their screw tactics, which resulted in Mather placing a second try to his credit after a good run, Bate making a good bid for goal. Barton afterwards made a long kick, the ball going in touch near the visitors' goal line. After a bit of give and take play Dykes scrambled over the line. Bird made a very good attempt at goal. Shortly after the whistle sounded, and concluded a good bard fought game, the score b-ing—Warrisgton 3 tries 3 minors, San- key 2 tries 1 minor. This is the first defeat of the Sankey team this season. 'Feams:—Sankey : Full back, Harding; threequarter backs, Woolley, Myles, and Barton ; half backs, Jefferson and Ashton; forwards, Dykes, Bird, Houghton, Barlow, Highley, Tonge, Hatton, Cooper, and Forster. Warrington Second: Davies, full back; Barlow. Bibby, and Mather, tbreequarter backs; J. Bate eod Boyle, half backs; Tbornley, Jones, Rigby, Bandies, Lloyd, Bate, Brown, Reyes, and Holmes, forwards. Umpires, &Man and Coyne; referee, Percy Fair. _

CVAriatteaTuie v. Mosseyor "A " Tmeats.—Thhe return fixture between these clubs was played at Warrington on Saturday. in favourable weather, before 1,500 spectators. It will be remembered that the Warrington men suffered their first defeat this season at Messley, and the home team were, therefore, determined to turn the tables when they Icame to Warrington, and this they succeeded in doing. Whittle won the toss, and Mason kicked off for Mosdey , against the wind. Dillon charging the ball down. A scrim- mage was formed in midfield. and Antrobus and Craghan re- moved play to the Moseley 25. The visiting forwards, hose- ever, soon tank play to the home quarters, Nevins saving two dangerous rushes. The Moseley front rank still con- tinued to press on, the ball eventually going touch in goal. Shortly after the drop out, Antrobus got hold and gained a lot of ground by a good run and kick, the oval reetiug in , touch in the Moseley quarters. Molyneux next obtained a free kick, but nothing came of it. Whittle here passed to Boardman, Marsden bringing him down near the line. Short rune by Thorpe, Booth, and o'l4ol removed play to the Warrington 23. Some good passing by Marsden, Thorpe, and Whiteley taok place, the latter player almost scoring. A scrimmage was formed, and the home team touched down. After the drop out Whiteley made an unsuccessful shot at goal. Warren now gained possessioniand made a splendid run, finishing up by kicking down the field, and Craghan following well up sent the oval into touch in the 'Moseley 25. Dillon, Heyes, and Telford were instrumental in re- moving play to the home line, where Kenworth pot in a good kick, and Whittle getting hold ran near the Mossley line and passed to Unsworth, this player having hard lines lin not scoring. Shortly afterwards Molyneux got over the ' line and gained a try, but the referee ruled the ball dead be- fore crossing the line, and a five yards scrimmage was formed. Warren passed to Antrobus, who transferred to Nevins, this player kicking to Booth, who returned to Jolley, who put in a splendid punt, and a scrimmage was formed Inear the Moseley line. Whittle here passed to Boardman, but Booth brought him down. Mason, Moorhouse, and Ben- nett cleared their lines. Ad imam and Heyes gained the lost ground, but the Moseley forwards, headed by Moorhouse, 'Bennett, and Batley, took play to centre, and O'Neill fur- ther improved matters by kicking into touch in the War- rington 25. Hackett received the ball from a line out, and dashed down the field, and on being tackled passed to Nevins. This player, after making a splendid run, transferred to Unsworth, who grounded the ball behind the posts, thus ' gaining a brilliant try. Boardman made a good bid for goal, but failed. This brought about half-time, the score standing—Warrington one try, Mossley two minors. Whit- tle re-started, but no return was made. The visitors, bow- ever, rushed the ball down the field, collaring Jolley before he could get his kick in. Kenworth and Jolley next ex- changed kicks. Whittle broke away with a dribble, and Unsworth further improved matters by taking the ball down , the field at his toes. Whiteley intercepted a pass from Warren. which was intended for Nevins, and made a short run. Unsworth, however, regained the lost ground, the ball going into touch near the grand stand. From the line out Heyes got hold, made a !mart rue, finishing up by passing I to Craghan, the latter, after a brilliant piece of play, ground- I ing the sphere over the line, hut this point was disallowed. Thorpe put in a good run, but was collared by Hackett. I Whittle next got clear away from the scrimmage, and made a grand run and p issed to the kome forwards, the oval rest- ing in the visitors' 25. Thorpe relieved by kicking to Jol- ley, who patio a fine punt, the ball going in touch in the, Moseley quarters. The Moseley forwards, after a short time, removed play to Ike Warrington 2:5, but Jolley was! equal to tLe occasion, and sent the ball into touch in the centre. Time was now called. Warrington winning by one try to Mossley two minors. The off-side play of Moseley somewhat spoiled the passin;, of the home Team, or the score would undoubtedly have been heavier. Teams : Warrington : Full back, Jolley ; three-quarter backs, Novins, ' Antrobus, and Boardman ; half backs, Warren and Whittle (captain); forwardn, Adamson, Craghan, Heyes, Dillon, Molyneux, Tolford, Unswerth, Hackett. and Eyes. Moseley: Full back, Kenworth ; three-quarter backs, Thorpe, White- ley, and O'Neill; half backs, Marsden and Booth; forwards, Moorhouse, Mason (captain), Dearnlev, Bennett, Mellor, Heald, Banks, Batley, and Hobson. WARRINGTON v. MOSSLEY.

The return match between these clubs was played on Saturday at Moseley. Ashton won the toss and elected to play with the hill in his favour. Meakin took the alternative of kicking off. Elough making but a poor return. Gilbert quickly led off with a dribble, then Wood passed nicely to Joe Winterbot- torn, who made little headway. The Warrington fqrwards worked with a will, and confined play to the home 25, but Meakin and CO2CO broke away, Massey picking up and -un- ning smartly back again. After give and take play, Jolley made a nice run, being collared on the line, a very good scrimmage being the next item. Ashworth relieved the tome citadel from danger, and Gilbert next dribbled nicely up the field. Speakman got over for the try, Fraik Tur- ner failing at goal, which was in rather a difficult p:sition.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY, 29. 1887..
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JANUARY, 29. 1887..

Fair Turner punted from the kick out, and play was con- fined to centre for some titne, Speakman in the end judi- ciously kicking to touch. Speakman next tackled Ash- worth twice in succession; Jolley doing the same for Win- terbettom. Meakin, at the bead of the home scrimmagers, broke away, and play was confined to the visitors' 25, bat Jolley returned to touch. Appleton next returned a good drop by Wisiterbottom, and Jolley intercepted a pass by the same player. Come bowled over Speak-man when a try seemed inevitable, and then the home forwards rushed up the field to Appleton, who cantered round his men, a miner being the result. At the finish of this piece of play Barnes returned the kick out, and Ashton and Davies collared Bil- hinge, another minor being the result of a good kick at goal by Barnes. The kick out was returned by H ugh, who shortly afterwards took one of Winterbottom's nooses, aod made headway. The play was now close to the home line, but this was quickly relieved, which brought about half- time, with the score one try two minors Warriagton to Mossley nothing. Crossing over Meakin made a poor re- turn, and for a snort time it seemed as if Warrington were going to score, but James Winterbottom, Meakin, and Cox got in a nice dribble, Corscadden farther aiding them by another dribble shortly afterwards. Marland VrAe now seen to advantage, frustrating the efforts of the half hicks to get at Billinge, who now passed finely, enabling Ash- worth to get in one or two nice dashes, play being confined to the visitors' quarters. Fair Turner and Gilbert removed, and Cox transferred to Lawton, who made a low but good bid at goal, thus scoring the first minor for Mossley. Mar- land next dashed away from the scrimmage, and the rest of the forwards aiding him, a scrimmage was formed on the line, where Billings was fortunate enough in getting over, Lawton kicking a beautiful goal. No return was made from the kick out, and play settled down close to centre. Gilbert next tackled finely, and a good loose scrimmage was wit- nessed. Baroes was next to the fore by a gold dodgy run, and Winterbottom replied with a nice kick. The home for- wards made a good rash, but Speakman saved finely. A good drop by Lawton followed, and Ashworth was instru- mental in bringing about another minor. From the scrim- mage at the 23. Billings again got bold, pretended to pass to Lawton, and then cleverly dodged the three-tparter and full back and planted the oval right behind the posts. Law- again being successful at goal. Another good run tiy Bil- lings, a nice dribble by Gilbert, and a good kick by Winter- bottom brought the game to a conclusion, with the score : Moseley, 2 goals 3 minor points; Warrington 1 try 2 minor points. Both lots of forwards played well, the home lot time after time being fortunate in the scrimmage in obtaining pos- session of the ball, this and the obstructive play of the wing men being greatly detrimental to any brilliant passing on the part of the Warrington half hacks. Billings deserves every praise for the game be played. Joe Wintenattom, Lawton. and Ashworth also played well. Jolley was the best of the trio of threelnarters, Barnes also playing a good game. The two halves did as well as emald be expscted, and Fair Turner, W. Dillon, Rigby, and Littlewood strove hard in the ranks of the forwards.

LIFERPOoL ELECTION. LIBERAL VICTORY. From 3,000 to 4,000 persons attended the meetings which were held on Monday evening at Lloyd's Repository, in furtherance of Mr. Neville's candida- ture, and the proceedings were characterised by, unanimity and the utmost enthusiasm. Amongst the speakers were Mr. W. Summers, M.P., Mr. C. M. Percy (Liberal candidate for the Inca Division at the last election, and the Rev. Griffith Ellis, M.A. luldressing a meeting of his supporters on Mon- day, at Liverpool, Mr. Goschen asked whether the I legislative independence which Irish leaders asked for on behalf of Ireland did not mean that the Irish Parliament was to be sovereign. In his opinion any such plan as that which was proposed by Mr. Glad- 'stone must lead the way to separation. On Tuesday afternoon, Mr. Goschen addressed a meeting of Liberal Unionists in Liverpool, which was influentially attended. Mr. W. 0. Alton pre- sided, and among those present were Colonel Hargrave Brown, M.P., Mr. W. E. Caine, M.P., and others. The polling for the representation of the Ex- change Division of Liverpool, rendered vacant by the recent death of Mr. David Duncan, M.P., took place on Tuesday, the candidates being Mr. Ralph I Neville (Gladstonian Liberal) and the Right Hon. G. J. Goschen, Chancellor of the Exchequer (I.TnioniAt and Conservative). The Exchange Divi- sion embraces five out of the sixteen wards of the city, viz., Exchange, Lime 7 street, St. Anne's, St. Paul's, and \ Vauxhall Wards, and the total number oT electors on the register is 7,911. This is a decrease of 260 voters as compared with the register of last year, when Mr. Duncan de- feated his ,Conservative opponent, Mr. L, R. Bally, by 170 votes, the numbers being'2,92o for Mr. Dun- can and 2,750 for Mr. Baily. There were five poll- ing stations appointed, one for each of the wards, and around each an eager crowd•collected by the time the poll opened at eight o'clock, and this was maintained during the whole of the day. The poll was an unusually heavy one in all the wards, and especially amoagst the Irish elec- tors, of whom something like 80 per cent. of those on the register went to the poll. The Conservativ as also polled heavily, and up to six o'clock they were pretty confident of being well ahead. From that time, however, until the close of the poll the Liberals came up with great steadiness, and when the poll closed there could be no satisfactory forecast .made as to the result, the anxious question being as to whether or not the votes for Mr. Neville given in the evening were sufficient to outweigh the Conservative gains in the earlier part of the day. But few cases of per- sonation occurred during the contest, only three or four arrests having been made for this offence. Amongst the prominent Liberals who worked hard for Mr. Neville were Mr. Robert Holt, Mr. Holder, Mr. T. P. O'Connor, M.P., Mr. Lawrence Connolly, M.P., Mr: O'Brien, M.P., Dr. Commins, M.P., and others; while equally active on the other side were Mr. A. B. Forwood, M.P., Mr. J. G. Gibson, M.P., and other leaders. At the close of the poll the ballot-boxes were conveyed to the Town Hall, where the counting at once commenced. An extra- ordinary scene took place at the counting of the votes. After several counts of the ballot papers, the result giving a narrow majority for Mr. Neville, the Mayor suggested a final count in the morning. This was obiected to by the agent of the Liberal candi- date, and the Mayor ordered another re-count, at the same time forbidding any one to leave the room, and a number of Press representative, who were in the ante-room were also prohibited from leaving. At the end of the counting the Mayor an- nounced that as there was still some doubt ,about one or two votes he would adjourn the final count natil 10 o'clock in the morning, when the official declaration will be made. The unofficial return is —Mr. Neville 3,222, Mr. Goschen 3,211, Liberal ma- jority 11. It was considerably after ten o'clock when the Mayor's decision was given. As soon as the unofficial result of the poll was made known to. Mr. Neville, the Liberal candidate appeared at the balcony of the Reform Club, Dale- street, which was densely crowded. When the long-continued cheering subsided he said he had told them they would have a hard fight, and so they had. (Cheers.) But he told them if they put their shoulders to the wheel they should win, and they had done so. (Cheers.) They had won their victory, and he thanked God for England, and he thanked God for Ireland—(cheers)—and he thanked God for himself. (Cheers.) Their opponents had been been beaten by a majority of eleven. (Cheers.) He was not going to brag about the victory they had won, but it would be a turning point between the nations of England and Ireland, and before twelve months were passed he hoped the two countries would be united heart and hand They had a very pleasant message' to send to their great leader—(cheers)---and he would be thankful to them for saving one of his strongholds in Liver- pool—(cheers)—and if they worked in the future as they did that day, no Tory membber of a Gov- ernment would be able to wrest the seat from them. Mr. Goschen was going back to Lord Salisbury empty-handed, and he (Mr. Neville) thanked them heartily for their efforts. (Cheers.) An immense crowd assembled in front of the Conservative Club-house, from which it was expec- ted that Mr. Goschen would address the ' electors. About nine o'clock Mr. Goschen entered the read- ing-room, and conversed with some of his friends. He then retired into the library to 'await the re- sult. The crowd waited with exemplary patience until after ten. All kinds of rumours were floating about, and giving a majority first to one candidate and then to another. At length, shortly after ten, a number of Conservative leaders arrived; and Mr. Alderman Livingstone, mounting a table in the reading-room, annottnced that the final count had been postponed till the following morning. He was afraid that as the count stood they were not victorious.—No other attempts at speech-making, was paade, and the crowd slowly dispersed. There were three re-counts, and after the clerks had finished six Conservative gentlemen went over the papers a fourth time. There were some papers in dispute, and after some discussion it was decided to defer the official declaration of the result until next day. The final count took place on Thursday morning, when the result was officially declared as follows : MR. NEVILLE 3,217 MR. GOSCHEN . 3,210
Majority

The match between Warrington and Moseley first teams on Saturday last P.,13 a good exhibition, although Ashton's lads did not show quite as good form as in the few pre- vious weeks' performances. It must be said that the run of luck seemed to be against Warrington, while on the other band Mossley were favoured in this respect. The cup• holders were at a loss for wing men, and thus the half hick play was somewhat spoiled by the oppos- ing men on the wing. A word of advice to the Warrington team, and that is, should they ever meet another club like Mossley play Fair Turner and Davies on the wing and have a good man for a pivot in the centre. The talk in football circles in Warrington this week has been about the matter contained in a Barrow newspaper in connectlon with the Barrow v. Warrington match. A writer, who styles himself "Referee," gives it as his opinion that Fair. Turner and Batnes are not so good as represented, and goes on to say that through the Warrington team hav- ing a club reporter their play has been brought before the public in a manner their merits are not entitled to. But what has been said of these two players has clearly a strong foundation in fact, when we consider that Barnes this season has scored seven dropped goals and seven tries; and that Turner has five tries to his credit, and all have been obtained in first-class matches. The committee of the Warrington Foothill Club think both players good enough to be nominated for county honours; they.have been considered good enough to assist the West Lancashire Union in their matches, and Mr. Sutton, no mean judge, has had them in his picked team. These are indisputable evidences of merit that most people will con- sider to far outweigh the opinions of a prejudiced itriter.

I We hear that Mr. Warren, the energetic secretary of the Warrington Club, has already arranged home and ho me matches with Dewsbury and Broughton. The Morsley " A " team proved themselves to be a smart lot of players when they visited Warrington on S aurday, ; and the encounter between them and Whittle's followers was of the most exciting description, the latter, however, managing through a piece of brilliant play on the part of Nevins and Unsworth to pat in the winning point. In this match Warren's re-appearance as a player on the Warring- ton ground was the cause of a good deal of interest, and on his turning out he came in for some warm applause. It was generally admitted that he still displays his former skill and judgment behind the pack, and he certainly did good service on several occasions en Saturday. . . -

One of tbe most foolish and least justifiable things foot- ball spectators can do is to hiss and boo:: at referees and urn- pires. This is done no doubt because spectators think jus- tice is not beirg meted out to the team they favour by the obnoxious official but it must be allowed by even the most enthusiastic of spectators in his calmer moments, that, as a general rule, nothing could be more impartial than the rul- ing of referees. In a game such as football, where the changes come so quickly and the ball at times travels back- wards and forwards so rapidly, it will, of necessity, be some- times next to impossible to come to an accurate decision,but this is cert.inly not the blame of the referee. As for the I umpires, they are expected to do the best they :an for the I teams they represent, and it is, to say the least of it, very foolish to hiss and hoot at them for merely doing what they are expected to do. The following ties in the second round in the West Lanca- ! shire Cup Competition have now been decided Lanes- shire Artillery Volunteers, a bye; Blundellsands, 11 points; Newtons 10 points; drawn ; Warrington Hornets, 27 points, St. Cleopes eight points! Wigan Rovers beat Lymm by 10 points to two ; Widnes St. Mary's beat Wigan St James's by 11 points to one; Batton beat Leigh by five tries alai nine minors, or 29 points to nil; Birkenhead Wanderers beat Standish South End by eight points to five; Pember-' ton beat Runcorn Recreation by 11 points to nil; Scott- lane v. Edgehill—Edgehill did not put in an appearance , until 4-30, and the referee awarded the match to Scott.• i lane. . In the Association cup tie, the meeting between Preston North End and Renton at Hanjpden Park. Glasgow, in the English cup competition, attracted no fewer than 10009 persons on Saturday. In the first half Rose, jun., scored the I first goal for the North End, and soon afterwards Gorden I obtained a second point. From this point to the finish ef the game the play was very even, and no further rroals were ' registered. The call of time thus left Preston North End I victorious by two goals to none.

LONDON, THURSDAY. The crowd of Liberals who thronged the benches to the left of the Speaker, in the House of Commons to-day, was plainly animated by a spirit long un- familiar. For three years at least I have not seen the Liberal party so Unaffectedly, jubilant as they were this afternoon. Certainly the session opens in circumstances very different from those which appeared probable so recently as a week before Christmas. The turning point was the resignation of Lord Randolph Churchill. Since then everything has gone well for the Liberal party, and everything badly for the Conservatives. Within twenty hours of the announcement of Lord Randolph Church- ill's resignation, Mr. Chamberlain made that unexpected signal of desire for reunion, which will, I venture to predict, lead to happiest results. Since • then misfortune hat steadily dogged the steps of the Conservatives, culminating to-day in the announcement of the defeat of Mr. Goschen at Liverpool. This is a quite unexpected triumph of the Liberal cause. Mr. Goschen and his supporters spoke hopefully of a majority of a thousand. The efforts of the Liberals were bent upon reducing that majority to the smallest possible limits, but they did not look to defeat tie combination of Conservatives and Dis- sentient Liberals which desperately championedlMr. Goschen's cause. This event, one of the chief topics of conversation this afternoon, has deeply depressed the Conservative party. Among Liberal chiefs the prevailing apprehen- sion is that the end will come too soon. The Gov- ernment, in deliberately declining to deal with the question of Local Government in Ireland, whilst they wave the red flag of a Coercion Bill before the infuriated Irishmen, simply commit an act of felo de se. With such a programme. they will be able neither to rule Ireland nor to control the House of Commons. A crisis must arise at no distant date, possibly even on the Addrest, and Lord Hartington's power to save them is grievously shaken by the defeat of Mr. Goschen at Liverpool. Mr. Gladstone , foresees the inevitable fall of the Government, and, differing in this respect from some of his trusted lieutenants, hails with enthusiasm the prospect of , once more appealing to the country. But even Mr. , Gladstone, if he Could control affairs,would def3r for • a while his own ret urn to power. In private conversa- tionhe is quite unreserved in the expression of the desire that Lord Hartington should have a ' turn of office before the Liberals come back to their heritage. "We have tried to settle the question of r Ireland," he says, "and have been defeated. Lord ; Salisbury has tried it and failed; now let Lord Hartington have a turn." Lord Hartington, I be- lieve, is not averse to such a proposal. I have heard from one of his councillors that when, in the first days of the year, Lord Salisbury made overtures to him involving his accession to the Premiership he was much inclined to take the office, and was dis- suaded only by his father, who did not relish the idea of seeing a Cavendish at the head of a Gov- ernment practically Conservative. If when Lord Salisbury's tottering Government comes to its fall Lord Hartington will undertake to carry on the business of the session, the attempt would be regar- ded with friendly interest by the Liberals. What , they fear is the Government being within the next few weeks defeated in the House of Commons and hastening on another General Election before the work of Liberal reunion is completed, and the coun- try has had a reasonably full opportunity of becom- coming familiar with the results of a spell of Tory Government.

RE-OPENING OF THE WARRINGTON LIBERAL CLUB. Within the last few weeks the premises of the Warrington Liberal Club have undergone consider- able alterations in the shape of improvements in ventilation and decoration, and on Monday evening the re-opening was celebrated by a tea and social gathering. The alterations may be briefly described as follows :—The large billiard room on the ground floor has had the whole of the woodwork through- out repainted, stained, and varnished, and the dado finished in a similar manner. The main walls of the room have been painted in a cinnamon colour, with ornamental border above the dado, and a frieze about eighteen inches deep at the level of the wall plate. Each bay of the ceiling has been divided ,into panels, having a light grey border with stencil pattern in the corner of each panel, the ground work of the ceiling being in cream colour. The refreshment bar and corridor on the ground floor have also been thoroughly renovated, and the whole of the wood-work painted and varnished. The walls have been completed in two colours— light buff and dark bet ithe wall spaces being divi- ded into panels. There is also an ornamental frieze below the cornice at the level of the ceiling. The main staircase and corridors have likewise been improved and adorned, having a dado of • chocolate colour, and ornamental stencil border on the top. The upper portions of these walls have been executed in a bluish grey tint, the effect being extremely light and pleasing, and it is enhanced by the light cradm colour of the ceilings. On the first floor, the private billiard room has also been, thoroughly overhauled. The whole of the woodwork has been grained and varnished, the walls have been • covered with sani- tary paper, and have a dado about five fleet high. The upper parts of the wall are covered with a pa- per of a light green that, and the ceiling with a cream c3loured sanitary paper. Throughout the decorations have given the club a very cheerful and attractive appearance, and both the design and exe- cution have been warmly admired. It should also be mentioned that both the large and the private billiard rooms have been thoroughly and satisfac- torily ventilated. The method adopted to accom- plish this is as follows: ample provision is made for the inlet of fresh air by tubes fixed in the wall above the dado, whiclican be' regulated as required; while over each billiard table are fixed small venti- lating pipes which carry the vitiated air of the room, and likewise the heat from the gas into one main shaft, communicating with an exhaust outlet fixed at the level of the ceiling, and carried through the roof. The whole of the work of ventilating and decorating has been designed and superintended by Mr. W. Perry, architect,Warrington ; the execution of the painting and decorating haying been entrus- ted to Mr. William Wareing, Academy-street, War- rington; and of We ventilating to Mr. Edward Wood, Red Bank Works, Manchester. Alike in de- sign and execution, everything has been, done in the most admirable style. At half-past six about seventy persons sat down to an excellent knife and fork tea. It was served in the assembly-room, and was in every res- pect a credit to the manager and manageress of the club, Mr. and Mrs. Mitchell. After tea there was a large gathering in the billiard room, Mr. John Crosfleld, J. P., presiding. Amongst those present were Alderman Burgess, J.P., Messrs. W. Pierpoint, F. A. Roberts, C. S. Burgess. J. IL Fleming, R. Roberts,l. Roberts, G. Plumpton, J. Walker, J. _ . _ _ _

People are beginning, to recover from the shock which followed upon the abrupt withdrawal by the "Daily News" of the curtain which veiled the movements of Germany and France. The foreign correspondents of the London journals, not influ- enced by the peculiar reasons swaying editors at home, have supplied in abundance from Berlin, Vienna, and Paris daily proof that the position was not one whit exaggerated in the statement pub- I lished last Monday morning. The calling out of the Austrian Landsturm ; the vote of 86 million francs by the French Chamber on the urgent demand of Gendral Boulanger; the order by the Austrian Go- vernment for a million pairs of soldiers' boots and wool for as many uniforms, "to be ready by the first of May ; " the clearing out of Australian meats from the London market by German agents; the French contract with- a Chicago firm for five mil- lion pounds of tinned meats; these, and a dozen other incidental facts, certainly do not look like a fixed belief in peace on the part of authorities best informed. The project of the Imperial Institute is scarcely any I more successful in the colonies than •at home. More than one of the richer colonies have under- taken to provide the solicited contribution. But it has been promised without anything i like enthu- siasm, and among the colonists there s angry talk about officials currying favour with Royalty and pledging colonial credit to serve their private ends. A much more pleasant incident in connection with colonial loyalty comes from the Cape. The Queen has just received a letter, written on behalf of the farmers of the Cape Colony, in which they beg her Majesty's acceptance of a dolman and fan of ostrich feathers, a rare and beautiful, present, which will doubtless be graciously accepted. This is much better than the touting for subscriptions among the colonial magnates and provincial mayors, who expect a knighthood at least in recompense of their services in directing the charity of others. The musical world is all agog with anticipation of the new opera by Verdi, which is to be brought out early in the coming month. The subject is Othello, and high anticipations of its success are formed. The composer has been engaged in the labour for fully a year, working regularly five hours a day. Next to music Verdi best loves agricultural pursuits. He is, in fact, apractical farmer, and likes to think that should music fail him he can take to

The CHAIRMAN, having remarked that the pro- ceedings that evening, &afar as speaking was con- cerned, would be'very short, because they had not come with the object of making speeches, said he wished to congratulate them on tile improved ap- pearance of that room and of the club generally. (Cheers.) He hoped that every member of the club would do his best to maintain it. (Hear, hear.) If each one of them would bring another member to the club they would have.a thousand members, and a club like that ought to have 'a thousand mem- bers. (Hear, hear.) The chairman then referred to the improvement in the room through the covering of the floor and the new ventilators, and said it was now a bright cheerful looking billiard room, and he trusted they would appreciate it. (Applause,'' Two games at billiards were then played between .Mr. Arthur Crosfield and Mr. John Crosfield, junr., and proved to be a most interesting feature of the evening's proceedings. Both of these gentlemen are exceedingly skilful plaYers, and their feats with thp cues were greatly admired, especially by those who indulge in the game. At the opening of the first game, Mr. John Crosfield, either owing to not being familiar with the table or nervousness did not score rapidly, though his strokes were Cleverly executed, and were generally within an ace of their mark. On the other hand, his brother played with ' steadiness and coolness from the beginning, and as a consequence, ran up a score very rapidly. The xesult was that when over, 100 points had been placed to the credit of Mr. Arthur Crosfield, Mr. ,John ,Crosfield's score stood at about half this num- ber. At this ,point, however, the latter gained ground very rapidly, and after some brilliant play. managed .to run out win- ner of a closely contested game.,. The second game was more evenly contested throughout, and ended in a victory for Mr. Arthur Crosfield. The score in both games was run up almost entirely by clever cannons and pockets, but later on in the evening Messrs. Crosfield played a game each with Mr. J. Calvert and Mr. G. It is,understood that proceedings for 're-opening the Colin Campbell divorce case hays been aban- doned, a determination the public will receive with sincere satisfaction. It would have been too much to have it all over again. The costs of the late ac- tion must have been enormous, sufficient to swamp the slender resources of both families. I hear that Mr. George Lewis declined to alcept more than costs out of pocket, an act of generosity which is at least in keeping with his character. The Queens- bury case passed over last Saturday with a brevity and swiftness upon which the Scotch courts are greatly to be ,congratulated. There was some talk recently of another case which was to eclipse in in- terest the Corm Campbell trial. It is now said that this has gone off, and for a moment the horizon is free from black clouds of this character. I believe that an attempt will be made in the coming session to carry a bill regulating thepuplication of evidence in divorce cases. But I doubt whether "it will suc- ceed. The matter is full of difficulty. When the Colin Campbell case first came before the courts it was, it will be remembered, heard in camera. I re- member the House of Commons was sitting at the time, town was full, and wherever two or three gathered together rumours and reports exaggerated or invented were circulated as to the proceedings behind the closed doors.

div.head: ettero to the editor.
div.p: ettero to the editor.
GOSCEIEN SOLD._

Sir,—For goodness sake -m-e -a little of your space, while I make a confession. If you don't I shall go mad. I had the required number, eight votes, to have given Poor Goechen his seat, and here, for a paltry 26 61,1 refused to go to Liverrool. Believe me or nor, if I had gone to that unhappy city I could have carried this number of votes to the booth. What stupidness on my part! I dare'nt tell it in Sankev-street, but let me breathe it in your ear, if only for my own peace of mind. I know also that our party, the Tories, bottled at least a hundred men on the river, and the pity of it is, they were Unionists. Oh, dear, dear ! TUE IRON.

WARRINGTON AM aLGAMATED SOCIETIES' MEDICAL ASSOCIATION. Sir,—After reading the report in your last issue of the meeting of the above association, there is one matter that I am desirous should be put tight. When I had read my re- port, several of the delegates pointed out an omission I had made in not making some -remarks as to the handsome manner in which the gentry of Warrington subscribed to the funds three or four years ago, when the association was in difficulties. The meeting was unanimous that the very hest thanks of all connected with the society were due to the gentry who at that time so generously subscribed to the funds. I shall be glad if you will kindly insert this in your next issue.—Yours truly,

I have heard some people complain of over-population. This is a very old complaint. Early in the century when bread was dear, work was often scarce, and people endured dreadful miseries. The explanation was that the country was over-peopled. "Philosopher, speculated upon methods for restraining the increase of the population, and they looked forward with hopeless despondency upon the con- stant growth of a population for whom already there was . not sufficiency of food. It seemed to many observers as if nature, like some poor men, was bringing into the world a larger number of children than she had the means to rear." At this time the population of Great Britain was about 20 millions. It is now over 35 millions, and the condition of of the people is happier to day than then, or than ever it was in our history. lam fully aware that trade is not near so good at present as it was 15 or 16 years ago. The state of trade then was quite phenomenal, and was owing in a I large measure to the Franco-German war. But because it l is cloudy to-day, is that any reason why the sun woe't j shine to-morrow?

Whoever hears of bread riots now-a-days, and people ab- solutely dying of hunger? What would friend "Cohn " think of respectable working-men having nothing better to wear en Sundays than fustian, and their wives and daugh- ters, aye, and farmers' wives and daughters, print dresses and straw bonnets? Not like the ladies and gentlemen they appear now. And what would he think of women and children working in coal pits. "dragging about little wag. goes by a chain fastened round the waist, crawling on hands and feet in the darkness of the mine?" Of children of six being habitually employed and working fourteen to sixteen hours a day? Of children of six being put to work . . ..

In the factories, and of their working thirteen to fifteen boors a day? The children often fell asleep at their work and were injured by the machinery, and the overlookers beat them severely to keep them awake. In those days working people were not allowed to combine or form them- selves into trade unions—at least not till 1824. An act was

in force compelling them to serve the first who asked them, and deterring them under pain of imprisonment from at- tempting to raise wages or reduce the hours of labour. They were taxed enormously. Bread was taxed, and sugar and tea, as were houses, windows, paper, and salt. "Paper was made to yield a revenue three times larger than the wages of all the people engaged in its manufacture." Newspapers were taxed 4d a copy. Working-men paid nearly one half their incomes in direct and indirect taxes and notwithstan- ding all the taxes, imperial and local, the condition of the towns and country was frightful. Drainage was unknown, and the filth of the cities lay festering on the streets. Gas was little known, and the streets were badly lighted with a few oil lamps. My authority for many of these statements is Mackenzie's " History of the Nineteenth Century," which I would cor- dially recommend •‘ Colin Clout" and his numerous friends to read. Any old people in Warrington will give him infor- mation as to the manner of living and the sanitary condi- tion of the town in the days I refer to. Thank God we live in happier times. I, for one, have no wish for a return to "the good old times when George the Third was King." The history of our country is a glorious one, but I believe that in the "good time coming" her past glories will be eclipsed by greater ones.—Yours, Warrington, January 27th, 1887. JOHN GANDY.

Warrington, Jan. 27th, 1887.
WARRINGTON RAGGED SCHOOL.

Sir,—Allow me to thank you —on behalf of the teachers, for the great interest you have taken in the Warrington Ragged Sunday School. We are still increasing in num- bers, both in children and earnest workers. On Sunday we had 227 scantily half-clad, and in many cases half-fed chil- dren, for many of them came without any dinner. There 13 a great difference in the cleanliness of them ; some are very dirty. We prevail on these to wash and clean them- selves, and if they have got no soap we have promised to get some for them, as cleanliness will add to the health and comfort of these poor, neglected children. It is a great work, sir, and we crave for help to make It a succoes. It is almost unbearable to see them in such a state. We thank those kind friends very heartily who have already given of their substance in money and clothing, but what are they among so many. We cordially invite any of our friends to pay a visit and see for themselves. On Sunday we were visited by Conncillor Dixon, Mr. Longdin, borough surveyor, who kindly addressed the children, Mr. P',ce, market inspector, Mr. Snethuret. and Mr. Biddle, who Waved earnestly for the poor children and their parents whom we intend to visit. Mr. Dale prevailed on the chit- I dren to ask their parents to attend Silver-street Mission, I which is for poor men and women who have not got 'decent Clothes to go anywhere ,Ise. Contributions will be thankfully received by yours truly, R. DACE. 53. Bewsey-street, treasurer. JAMES SKELLAND, superintendent. BUTLER and OSBORNE, secretaries. Warrington, January 20,886. THE UNEMPLOYED AND THE DISTRESSED. Sir.—ln writing the following, I have no desire to cast blame on anyone. because I know a great deal has been done by private individuals ; neither do I wish it to be in- ferred that I want to receive the slightest prominence in the matter. I will go to the subject at once. The first ques- tion I would ask is —"ls there any distress in the town or not?" The next is—" Has there been anything done to relieve it ?" It has been stated that an enquiry office ex- ists somewhere, at which the balance remaining from last year's distress fund will he used to relieve any deserving person. As a subscriber to that fund, I claim a little right to enquire. Last year our respected Ex-Mayor, Mr. Alder- man Harrison, gave valuable weekly reports of what was done and how the money was spent. In vain have I looked for the first report from the Committee left to deal with this fund as to what has been done up to now. Perhaps they are waitfng for some great demonstration, as in other towns on the part of the unemployed, before taking action, or per- haps the weather has not been severe enough. If prophesy proves true, we are to have a continuance of such weather as we have had lately, the little help that the wealthy amongst us might now give to help those who may be in diffi- culties to tide over their distress, might perhaps in two or three weeks tirne prevent the unseemly demonstrations which are now being witnessed in other towns by the unemployed, led on by agitators ever ready to handle them, and encour- age them to plunder and to rob. "The poor against the aristocracy," they would term it. Yen may depend upon I it, Mr. Editor, private charity at the present time is help- to break the back of the great distress amongst us, or more would be heard of it, but this cannot go on amongst a few, and therefore the object of this short let- ter is to ask those who are well-to-do amongst us whe- ther it is not to their interest to early consider the ques- tion, and so prevent the cry, —"You are the poor and starving, and these are the rich."—Yours truly, S. DAVIES. Warringfon, January 20th 1987.
"WAIT A LITTLE LONGER."

--- Sir,—l read with considerable interest the letter of" Colin Clout" in your issue of Saturday last, and I particularly noticed his remarks about the Sankey Sugar Works; 50 men baying been turned away from their employment owing to the introduction of UM and improved machinery. He then remarks that" me and two or three hundred friends of mine are getting just a little bit bothered with this new and patent machinery. The blessings we are receiving from it are so numerous, and come and go se quickly, that we are really unable to grasp them. The consequence is we altogether miss them, and are being left floundering in the ditches, where you will find as one of these days feeding on nettles like the poor wretches in Ireland." Now, sir, such expressions are quite unworthy of one so evidently intelli- gent as" Colin Clout." They don't speak much for his knowledge of history. I always sympathise with the lot of poor peop e, and I think their condition might be be greatly ameliorated. At the same time I believe most emphatically that a process of amelioration of their condition is constantly going on, and, in spite of all that croakers may say, the condition of the masses of this country is better to-day than it was fifty and sixty years ago, and infinitely better than it was in the earlier years of the century. Professor Huxley said the other night in the Mansion House that we were entering, Or had already entered, upon an industrial war that was likely to be more disastrions In the closing years of the cen- tury than the military wars of the commencement of the century. Al the risk of being thonght very rash and im- prudent, I modestly venture to differ from ?von so great a man. Without doubt he is a great authority in his own domain of science, but lam afraid 11Is.comrnercial opinions are worth about as much as his political ones. I grant that we are having a vast amount of Competition and being a tradesman, I have, unfortunately, a more intimate acquaint- ance with it than is at all agreeable to myself. But, sir, I contend that people are better off to-day than they were tifty ersixty years ago, and that they are so, mainly owing to the introduction of new and improved machinery. Let "Cohn Clout " enter into conversation with a few old people of the poorer class ; let him ask them what the rate of wages was when they were young, what were the prices of bread, meat pota- toes. sugar, tea, coffee, clothing, &c. Let him compare the purchasing power of the money earned then and now, and I venture to. believe that he will take a more cheerful and grateful mew of things as they now are.

OUR FINANCIAL LETTER. [FROM OCR OWN CORRESPONDENT.] 23, Old Broad-street, E.C. The Steck Fxcl3ange at the beginning of the week was I the victim of a scare without parallel for many years. The Russian scare some two years ago was more gradual, but ' the effect of last Monday's panic was not only sudden in its effect, but the cause was undoubtedly one of the most dis- graceful within the memory of the oldest member of the Stock Exchange, and when it is reported that the authors of the scare were gainers to no less a figure than half a million of money, sufficient condemnation cannot be ex- pressed in ordinary language, especially when the paper which has been regarded as the embodiment of all sobriety allows its columns to be used for the most despicable of pur- poses. The settlement which commenc-d on Tueeday witnessed a strong rise from the previous day's panic, and carrying over pricm were therefore more favourable than would otherwise have been. Fortunately bons fide investors need not suffer from such unexpected falls as were occasioned by the panic, as few would attempt to realise at such a period, as the very fact of holding on to their stock gives a firm- ness to the market which if fully maintained will re-act in favour of the holders. The general absence of all genuine business on the part of the brokers is evidenced by the small amount of the settlement, which is unusually limited; the redeeming feature of which is the generally improved dividends declared by the leading banking houses and railway companies; and the Datuml inference is that the long looked for improvement in trade is beginning to manifest itself. Two more railways have declared their dividends, viz., the South-Western and the Chathatn and Dover, the South-Western at the rate of oi per cent., and the Chatham 41 on its preference stock, the latter being a quarter per cent, better than the previous year. There were two companies before this week which inves- tors should exhibit extreme caution before investing in— they are the Automatic Match Machine Company and Edgecumbe Rent Company—the former is one of a series of automatic boxes for ebtaining matcbee, and for which the inventor is to receive no less a sum than £38,000 ; as the chief feature of this machine is its novelty, the clauses of any permanent dividends are very remote. The latter company is to take over a glazing process for railway sta- tions, the reasons given for the conversion being the desire of one of the partne.s to retire and the death of another. Before investors have anything to do with either they should satisfy themselves on the nature of the contracts.
LECTURE ON NATIONAL DEBTS.

Under the auspices of the Warrington Liberal I Club Debating Society, a lecture was given last evening, in the Co-operative Hall, by Mr. Thomas Snape, of -Liverpool, on "Our National Debts, how they are made, and when they are paid." The chair was taken by Mr. John Croslield, J.P., who was supported on the platform, in addition to the lec- turer, by Mr. Thomas Crosfield and Mr. Richard Eastley (of the Liverpool Peace Society), Mr.- J. T. Marsh (secretary to the Liverpool Peace Society), Messrs. A. Rathbone, H. Roberts, H. Whitham, S. Kenyon, S. Dunbobbin, W. Crosskill, D. Davies, and T. Pemberton (secretary to the Liberal Club Deba- ting Society). There was a laze attendance. The CHATHMAN, who was received with applause, said that he thought himself that if there was one question more than another that desired the atten- tion of the people of England it was the question of our wicked and wasteful expenditure. He was. very pleased to see such a large number of gentle- men present. Lately he had taken a great deal-of interest in the question of expenditure, and, as he had said Several times before, it was a wonder to him that the people of Eng- land did not open their eyes, and did not rise as one man and go and knock down the doors of the House of Commons, and tell the Go- vernment that they would stand it no longer. (Cheers.) He said that to Mr. John Bright— (cheers) —three weeks ago. Mr. Bright replied, "I said years ago that the best thing that could happen to, this country would be that the Foreign Office should‘be burned down, and everything that was in it." That meant that, in Mr. Bright's opinion there was still too much meddling in foreign affairs by the Eng- lish Government. (Cheers.) We were not the policemen of Europe. (Laughter and cheers.) It was not the business of the people of England to be fighting other people's battles. No Government in this country had a right to be shedding the blood of Englishmen, and spending the treasure of the country, in fighting battles on the Continent. There had been too many of these wicked wars. Many in that room were old enough to remember the Crimean war. There never was a more wicked or more unjustifiable one than that. It cost 40,000 English lives and 100 millions of English money to blow down Sebastopol, and when it , was done England was not one bit the better off. (A ' voice: "Two guns in Warrington.") Within two or three years Sebastopol was built up again, and, there it was now just as before. Would they believe that the cause of that war was the question of whether candlesticks should be on the altar of the 'church. (Laughter.) Then there was the Afghanistan war. It was just as wicked, and just as unjustifiable. The Zulu war was every bit as bad. And last, there was the lamentable Egyptian war. It made him blush for his country when he thought of a nation professing Christanity entering into that wicked and unjustifiable war. Let them think of the expenditure upon our Army and Navy. What was the use of those great, thundering iron- clads? None; except to sink each other, and they cost nearly a million of money each. There were two of them now ready to be launched, and then England would be safe. (Laughter.) His opinion* was that the bombardment of Alexandria was noth- ing but a test to see what the ironclads could do, and a nice mess it led to. It was said.that the ob- ject of the war was to protect the Suez Canal, but it was just as safe before the war as now. They would find that the majority of these laws generally began from a trifling thing that was of no consequ- ence whatever. If they did not stop that sort of thing it would be the ruin of the country. (Hear, hear.) In the United States, with twice the population of Great Britain, the expenditure was 10 millions a year, and in England it was 90 mil- lions. ("Shame.") In consequence England was losing in the race, and would very soon have to take a back seat, and play second fiddle. A gun of 100 tons cost £100,000„ and it cost .£l2O every time it was fired; they might well have an income-tax of 8d In the Were he Chancellor of the Exchequer he would soon reduce the expenditure by 20 millions a year—(cheers)—and would do away with the in- come-tax and a good many taxes too. He wished there was some young fellow of about thirty who would visit the large towns, and wake up the people on this question by giving them figures, and showing how foolish and how wicked these wars were.: No war was justifiable except that of self- defence, and a "spirited foreign policy" siinily meant meddling with other people's disputes. (Hear, hear.) The Tories told them that they should protect their own country. Well, they 'all wished to protect their own country, but there was no need to do it with that enormous expenditure. If any army were to attempt to come to the shores of England they would only be too glad to get back again if they could get back. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) But he could tell them it was an enor- mous task to move 20,000 men across the British Channel, and there was no more fear of any conti- nental nation sending an army here than there was of this country attacking the United States. It was all moonshine. (Laughter.) •The grandest thing to prevent war was commercial intercourse. (Hear, hear.) Let them look at the commercial inter- course between England and the ,United States; the two nations were so bound to each other that there was no statesman in this country dare talk about war with America, and the most sensible thing this country ever did was to settle the dispute about the Alabama by arbitration. (Applause.) We paid three and a half millions of money in connection with that dispute, and he had been told by an American gentleman that a president of the United States had said that that arbitration was the finest thing that had ever been done in the history of nations, although the damage done to America in her trade and shipping was not less • than twelve hundred millions of dollars. The Alabama was built by a Tory at Birkenhead, and he had the audacity to stand up in the House of Commons, and the House of Commons was so rotten as to cheer him when he said he would rather be the builder of twenty Alabamas than he would be Mr. Bright, who did nothing but set class against class. That man ought to have been hooted out of the House, and his name should be execrated for making such a speech. (Loud applause.) Mr. SNAPE, who was received with loud applause, said that last year the English National debt amounted ins round sum to £748,716,000. A large portion consisted of the funded debt, or what was often called consols. £17,603,000 was unfunded debt or debt that could be paid off at once.' Then there were terminable annuities amounting to £85,830.000, and the Government held money through the savings' bank to the extent of £2,133 000, and there w%re other liabilities which the Government had in connection with courts of justice amounting to £4 300,000. In 1751 it was determined to consolidate the whole of the various loans that had at that time been made to Government, and that was the oriein of the funded • debt which was known as the consolidated debt, or consols, as it was now known for short. The debt commenced originally by what was called the King's debt, in 1688, when it stood at the comparatively small sum of £664,000, so that 200 years ago the nation had to deal with a sum that could eaaily ha7e been cleared off. After the peace of Utrecht, when the wars with France had practically terminated, the debt amounted to £12,600,000. In 1714. however, they had been engaged in further wars, conducted by the Duke of Marlborough, and the debt rose to £36,000,000. The country was so grateful to the Duke of Marlborough for haring landed it into this enormous augmentation of debt that a Jaw was passed that he and his heirs, males, should have a pension for ever of £4,000 a year, and until a year or two ago they bad been pay- ing to the successive Dukes of Marlborough that very hand- some sum for getting them so handsomely into debt. (Laugh- ter.) A year or two ago, however, Mr. Bradlaugh—(ap- plause)—had been making the Marlborough family a little bit alarmed as to their pension, so it was commuted for £102,000. Now they wore no longer pensioners, but they had that £lO2 000 to deal with as they please. Through the Seven Years' War the debt rose to £133,000,000, and the war against the Americans when they fought for inde- pendence brought it up to £273,000,000. In the peace which ens4ed after that war there was a reductioo in the debt of £3,400 000. (Laughter.) Through interference in the French revolutionary quarrel, the Peninsular war, &c., the debt sprung up to the enormous sum, in 1815. of £902.000,000. In thirty - nine years between 1815 and 1854 mere progress was made in diminishing the debt than bad ever been made before, and it was brought down to £800,000,000. The Crimean war, however, broke out, and a more infamous, blundering, miserable war, could scarcely have been entered upon, and that war cost this country £lOO.OOO 000. (Hear, hear.) That war cost the whole of the countries engaged in it £340,000,000, and Mr. Kinglake, the historian of the war, estimated that it coat directly and indirectly no fewer than a million of human lives. Yet Lord John Russell admitted that the war was a blunder, and that it might have been avoided. That war increased their debt to £834,000,000, but by 1870 they succeeded in wiping off the £34,000,000, and since then to bring it down to the figure at which it at present stood. The !ecturer next referred to the enormous amounts that had been paid in interest on the national debt, and also to the indebtedness of other nations. The lecture was listened to with great attention, and at its conclusion Mr. Snap@ was very loudly applauded. On the motion of Mr. T. CROSFIELD, seconded by Mr. T. Blaciatt, and supported by Mr. MARSH and Mr. Wurre mast, a hearty vote of thanks was accot ded the lecturer. A similar vote to the chairman brought the meeting to a close.
