div.head: SEQUEL TO THE JEWISH MARRIAGE
div.p: SEQUEL TO THE JEWISH MARRIAGE
AT WIDNES.

Before Mr. G. Pilkington and Mr. H. Gaskell, junr., at Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Robt. Herriman, landlord of the Mersey Hotel, was charged with having on the 14th inst. kept open the hotel for the sale of intoxicating liquors during prohibited hours. He was further charged with having on the same occasion allowed divers persons to play billiards on the premises. The defendant was represented by Mr. George W. Rideal, of War- rington, and pleaded not guilty.—P.S. Robinson deposed that at 25 minutes past three on the morn- ing of the 14th instant he found tha door of the Mersey Hotel open, and on entering he found a number of persons there. A barman named Jones was supplying drink. At a later hour he again visited the premises, accompanied by P.C. Cum- mings, and the persons were still being served with liqhor. On this occasion he saw the defendant and a person named Steinhart, and he asked for an ex- planation. Steinhart replied that the people were his guests, and whatever they drank he would pay for it. The landlord confirmed this assertion. He asked Mr. Steinhart how he had invited the guests, as he did not seem to know them all, and he re- plied "by card." In cross-examination Sergeant Robinson said amongst those present he knew Geo. Mellon, William Melvin, Ellis Sankey, and Samuel Gandy. The class of people there was very respec- table.—Mr. Rideal: Dr. 0 Keeffe, Dr. McDonnelLthe Rev. Alexander, myself, and a party of others. Wit- ness: Yes.—Mr. Herriman told him there had been a Jewish wedding there, and he thought he was carrying on the affair according to a permission he had received from Inspector Wood.—P. C. Cum- mings corroborated.—ln addressing the Bench for, the defence, Mr. Rideal said on the 13th instant a friend of Mr. Steinhart's, and one of the same reli- gion, was married. Previously, the brother of the bride, Mr. S. Claff, furniture broker, Ann-street, Widnes, saw Mr. Herriman with regard to having a number of rooms in the Mersey Hotel set apart for the ceremony, and the festivities that would follow. Before giving permission Mr. Merriman saw Inspector Wood; and he contended that there had not been a tittle of evidence brought forward to show that the defendant kept his house open. The house was closed at eleven o'clock, and only members of the wedding party remained, and all that was supplied was supplied by Mr. Claff, the brother to the bride. There was not the slightest intention to break the law, and he asked their wor- ships to allow the case to be withdrawn on payment of costs.—Dr. O'Keeffe was called, and stated he was invited to be present at the defendant's house on the occasion of the wedding between Miss Claff and Mr. Blank. He went there about two o'clock on the afternoon of the 13th, and remained until about two o'clock next morning. He was there as the guest of Mr. Claff, and partook of the good things provided. He proposed, the health of the bride and bridegroom. He saw no persons except the wedding party present after eleven o'clock.— Cross-examined by Superintendent Barker: He had some of the National beverage—lrish whiskey. (Laughter.) He did not pay for anything during the whole day.—Alexander Attwell, county court bailiff, said he and his wife were also guests. The house was closed at eleven o'clock. The defendant told him that so long as the guests kept in the rooms engaged by Mr. Claff they could stop until morning. His wife was rather delicate, and being cold when just on the point of departing at four o'clock, he asked the defendant to supply her with a small whiskey hot, but he replied that he could not, as the house was closed.— By Superintendent Barker: He was not drinking at the expense of Mr. Merriman, but at the expense of the wedding party during his stay.—Samuel Claff, furniture broker, Ann-street, Widnes, and also in Runr.,orn, said he was the brother of the young lady that got married on the 13th. After Mr. Hem- man had seen the Inspector of Police,.he engaged at the Mersey Hotel the dining-room, the kitchen, the sitting-room, the ball-room, the billiard-room, and 4 bedrooms. Friends were present from Widnes and all parts of the country, and he paid for everything which was supplied. The house was closed at eleven o'clock, and only the wedding party re- mained. Several of the party staved for breakfast. There were several doctors, a nutaber of tradesmen, and others present.—The Solicitor contended that the party was entirely a private one, and therefore no offence had been committed.—The Bench retired to consider the case, and on returning into court, Mr. Pilkington said they thought there was a breach of the law, but they we not disposed to inflict more than a nominal penalty. They wished it to go forth to the public that such things would not be allowed, and that any further case of a similar character would be severely dealt with. The defen- dant would have to pay a fine of lOs and costs.— Superintendent Barker said he had no objection to withdraw the summons for billiard playing on pay- ment of costs. Publicans should understand that billiards could not be played even by lodgers after closing hours.—Mf. Rideal: I am much obliged to the Superintendent for withdrawing that case. We will pay costs. . .

At an Inquest at Hampstead, on Tuesday, a verdict df wilful murder was returoed against Eliza Aloner, domestic servant, who is alleged to have cut off the head of her illegi- timate child, shordy after its birth. On Wedneedy afternoon an explosion of gas. due to con- tact with a naked light, occurred in the Bolton colliery of Messrs. Scrowcroft and Sons. Two men were seriously burned, but fortunately the other miners in the pit were able to escape without injury. GAOL DELIVERY.—On Wednesday a deputation from Lancashire waited upon the Home Secretary and urged that an alteration should be made In the arrangement by which judgcs made a complete gaol delivery when they get on circuit, instead of leaving minor cases for Quarter Sessions to dispute of. Mr. Matthews said that a bill had been drafted by his predecessor, and he Imed that a measure might be introduced if there were time this session. THE FATAL GAS EXPLOSION AT PORTSMOUTH BARRACKS. —The Inquest on the bodies of the five soldiers who were killed by a gas explosion at Portsmouth Barracks, was re- sumed on Tuesday, when the Coroner summed up. The jury, after an hour and a half's deliberation, returned a verdict of " Accidental death," and added the following rider :—" We consider the present system now laid down by the Government military authorities for the regulation of gas in their department most unsatisfactory, and ought to be forthwith altered." .

- MURDERS BY MARRIED WOMEN. - At Manchester Assizes, on Tuesday, two women were indicted for mur- der, and were ordered to be detained during her Majesty's pleasure. A married woman named Crean, who had pre- viously been in the asylum, cut the throat of her daughter, three years of age, at Salford, and afterwards attempted to commit suicide, while of unsound mind. Another mar- ried woman, named Urance, was indicted for murdering her infant daughter, at Aspull, and evidence was ,given that she was unable to plead. Both were remanded to the amy•

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

Mr. Parnell has drafted an amendment to the Address 1 raining the agrarian question in a general form. The men employed at Preston Grange Colliery, in the east I co, Scotland, started work on Friday at an advance of six- ' pence per ton. Sir John Lubbock intends taking vigorous action during the present session with the object of securing an improve- ment in the currency. The nomination for the Dartford Division of Kent. where Sir Wm. Hart Dyke is seeking re-election on his joining the Ministry, is fixed for Wednesday next. iTwo thousand fn,n at go,ckow Vaughan's Ironworks Middlesborough, intend striking to-day for 10 per cent ad- vance. The directors threaten to close the works. The Duke of Devonshire has given to the Corpora- tion of Keighley several acres of valuable land for the . purpose of a public park. The value of the land is stated ' to be £l,OOO. I It is now stated that, as there is DO probability of a va- cancy securing in the representation of Oxford University, there is no truth in the report that Mr. Goscben is going to stand for that constituency. IMPROVED TRADE.—The return of American foreign trade for 1886 shows that the exports amounted to 713,289,666 dole. and the imports to 663,417,210 dots. As compared with the previous year's return, the exports increased 25 , millions, and the imports 75 millions. THE VACANCIES IN IRELAND.-00 Friday, the Speaker's warrants to issue writs for North Antrim, Mr. Macnaghten having been appointed Lord of Appeal, and for North Long- ford, Mr. Justin M'Carthy having chosen to sit for Derry, were received at the Hanaper Office. Dublin, and the writs were sent respectively to the sherlif of each county. GREAT COTTON FIRE AT LIVERPOOL—About nine o'clock on Friday morning a certified warehouse in Duke- , street, Liverpool, was found to be on fire. The building , contains cotton and robber lia the value of over £50,000. At , the time of telegraphing the fire was burning fiercely, al- , though steam and other engines had been playing on it for ; some hours. . THE LtmtrED Lreletrxry Anr.—On Friday afternoon a . very large deputation, composed mostly of members of Par- , !lament, waited upon the Prime Minister and the Chancellor , of the Exchequer at the Foreign Offic,f, to urge the neces- sity of making certain alterations in the Limited Liability Acts. Lord Salisbury said the Government would do their utmost to provide a remedy for the evils the deputation had . laid before them. 1, THE GLENREIGH EVICTIONS.—The eviction party made . another start at half-past nine o'clock on Friday morning, . in delightful weather. They were accompanied by the crow- bar men, which was an ominous s:gn that Mr. Roe intended • to level the houses of those who at the last moment refused ; to pay. Coomasaharn was the place to be visited, and it i was understood that Friday's business would bring the - present campaign to a close. ' , THE PRINCE OF WALES AS LORD RECTOR. —. The Stu- dents' Liberal and Conservative Associations of the Edin- burgh University have unanimously agreed to ask the ; Prince of Wales to allow himself to be nominated as Lord Rector of Edinburgh University, in succession to Lord Iddesleigh. The Prince is an old alumnus of the Uni- versity, and the students feel that his election would l be peculiarly appropriate in this her Majesty's Jubilee L I year.

div.head: SPITALFIELDS DISASTER.
div.p: THE SPITALFIELDS DISASTER.

The adjourned inquest on the bodies of the seventeen victims of the Soitalfields disaster was opened at Shoreditch Town Hall on Friday. Abraham Smith, manager of the Dramatic Club wheae the catastrophe occurred, deposed that about 400 people were present on the night in question, and that all went well until some one raised an alarm of tire. The audience became involved in inextricable confusion. The Coroner was then handed a copy of the club rules, which he read. Mr Smith, continuing his evidence, said be had engaged a constable a month ago in consequence of a threat that a gang of roughs would attack the place, but the constable was away that evening, as he bad not anticipated any disturbance. He believed the premises had passed the dis- trict surveyor. About two minutes after the gas was ex- tinguished some of the lamps were re-lit. No one was specially appointed to look after, the gas. In answer to questions from those representing interested parties, witness said the whole burden ef conducting the affair fell upon him. A man whom he named, belonging to a rival club, had threatened to force his way ioto the place and burn it down. After the conclusion of Smith's evidence, the sec- retary was examined in reference to the rules of the club, which the Coroner thought were somewhat mixed up.—An architect was then called, and stated that the accommoda- tion was—body of the hall 474 persons, gallery 248 —Abra- ham Groseberger, barman, stat-d that the cry of fire Came from the gallery opposite the stage.—Some further evidence having been given, the jury was again adjourned.

GERMANY, BERLIN, FRIDAY AFTERNOON. It is stated that the German military authorities, as a counter move to French concentration on be frontier, have ordered the erection of barracks, for the accoorno3ation of German troops, at cr. tam n points Rear the frontier.
Mr. W. H. Smith and Mr. Goschen had interviews with Lord Sall 'bury at the Foreign Office, on Friday.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT.

HOUSE OF LORDS. ARMY EXPENDITURE.—Lord WEMYSS asken whether the Government were taking any and what steps to improve on, military armaments and organisation.—Lord NORTHBROOK stated that the increase in naval and military estimates was due to two preceding Liberal Governments; and, having regard to exisisting contracts, Lord G. Hamilton could not now reduce expenditure.—Earl GRANVILLE generally en- dorsed this statement—Lord Harms replied that the selec- tion of rifle for the army had nearly been arrived at. The defence of coaling stations and ports was being pushed for- ward as fast as possible. There was no Intention to reduce the volunteer forces.—The House then adjourned.

div.head: HOUSE OF COMMONS.
div.p: HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Noneus, Concm-on—ss.;;;—;l'i was issued for South Sligo —Mr. ROBERTSON gave notice to call attention to and move a resolution for the abolition of the Parlia- mentary representation of the Universities of Oxford and Cambridge.—Mr. BROADHURST gave notice to call attention to the subject of the taxation of ground rents.—Sir J. GONST. replying to Mr. Cramer, said the district in the ruby mines of Burmah had been occupied by Her Majesty's forces without opposition, l'usi VOLUNTEER FORCE.—Mr. STANHOPE, replying to Mr. Howard Vincent, said the report cf the inquiry into the volunteers' grievances had been received. It recommended under certain conditions the increase of the capitation grant. He had not had time to consider the report. CANADIAN FISHEBIE9.—Sir. J. FERGUSON, replying to Mr. Morgan, said the Government were in communication with the Government .of the United States on the question of the Canadian Salines. A despatch just received gave good ground for anticipating a permanent satisfactory set- tlement of the dispute.

Tins GLENBEIGH EVICTIONS.---Sir M. BEACH, replying to Mr. Theodore Fry, said the Government had no power to take steps to prevent the burning and levelling of cottages at Glenbeigh. He thought the best thing to be done would be to remove Ike poor people from noverty-stricken districts to other parts of Ireland.—Several Irish members calling "Shame," the SPEAKER intimated that such a term was unparliamentary, and if used he should take notice of it. COAL MINES.—Mr. H. MarraEws, replying to Mr. Burt, said the Government intended introducing a Bill to consoli- date Mines Regulations Acts. LIVERPOOL ELECTION —Mr. Neville took his seat for Liverpool (Exchange Division) amid loud cheering. THE ADDRESS. _ . . .

- The adjourned debate on the Address; was resumed. Col. I Sanderson defended the Irish landlords from the charge of being rapacious. He admitted Ireland was comparatively I free from crime, but the battle now going On was whether ' the law of lend was to be paramount. The Land Bill of 1881, he thought, had laid the foundation for a settlement of the land question, although its author did not appear to place much confidence in it, by giving the ten- ants a stake in the country, and an interest 1 in the maintenance ef peace and order.—Mr. T. HAR- RINGTON defended the action of the National League.— Mr. BARTLRY was of opinion that the blame for the misery caused by the evictions of tbe Glenbeigh tenants must ulti• mately rest on the member for West Kerry and his friends. With regard to economy, he felt certain that by careful expenditure an enormous reduction in cur national expendi- ture might take place. If the late Chancellor of the Ex- chequer had been sacrificed on the altar for economy and thrift, he would have, like the grand old martyr of old, lit a candle which would not soon be Out out.—Sir T. ESMOND contended that it was as lawful for the Irish tenants to com- bine against landlords as for workmen to combine against employers. Ile denied that the plan of campaign was a scheme to enable the Irish tenant farmer to evade his legal obligations. He supported the plan of campaign as an Irish landlord who desired to act fairly to his tenants.—Mr. C. GREY hoped the farmers of England would never attempt to benefit themselves by laving their hands on the property of others.—Mr. O'HRA defended the action of the tenant ! farmers of Ireland —General DAVIS protested against the length of time devoted to the discussion of the Irish question and expressed a hope that the Government would see their way to improve countervaling duties on bounty fed goods. Mr. N..lan thought the best way of remedying time being consumed in discussing Irish questions was to allow the 1 Irish people to manage their own affairs.—Mr. FCLTON, while designating the Land Purchase Bill as a monstrous political abortion, ascribed the defeat of the separatist party at the last election to the proposal to hand over the govern- ment of Ireland to the apostles of public plunder. Mr. Txmonoex FRY condemned the proceedings at Glenbeigh, and expressed surprise at the declaration of the Irish Chief Secretary that it was not his business to express any opinion on the subject. The debate was continued by Sir M. Beach and fives thee adjourned on the motion et Mr. BRADLALGII. —The House adjourned at 45 minutes past 12.

div.head: DIRECTORS' REPORT.
div.p: DIRECTORS' REPORT.

The report of the directors was as :—" The direc- ters, in submitting to the shareholders the annual balance sheet, certified by the auditor, have to report that the posi- tion and prospects of the business continue to be in every way satisfactory. Including £15,281 9s 41, brought from previous account, the net balance of profits, af- ter providing amply for all bad and doubtful debts, and rebating the current bills at five per cent, is £119.307 Is 7d. The distribution of this sum, 'recommended by the directors, is as fellows :—ln- terim half yearly dividend, at 15 per cent per annum, de- clared 23d July, £42,000; dividend to be now paid at the rate of 15 per cent per annum, free of income tax. £42,000 ; bonus of lOs per share, free of income tax,!£l4,ooo ; to pro- perty account, £5,000 ; balance to next account, £16,307 Is 7d. The directors who retire at this time by rotation are Mr. Edward Greenall, the Right Hon. Lord Delarnere, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Bart., M.P., Sir Tomas G. Frost, Mr. John Thompson, and Mr. Peter Stubs, all of whom are eli- gible and are recommended for re-election.—The CHAIRMAN, in moving the adoption of the report, said he might once more congratulate them upon the very satisfactory balance sheet they had to submit. Its main features were very much the same as that of last year, but if there was any variation it was probably on the side of improvement, and therefore in the right direction. (Hear, hear.) Although the year began gloomily enough, and in January last there were little signs of revival, still as the year wore on a better feeling seemed ta prevail, and more activity was apparent in some of the leading trades and a general hopefulness seemed to pervade the commercial classes that the worst was over, and that the re-action was , impending. As they knew he had always avoided indul- ging in prophecies at their annual meeting, but he was only I following in the wake of a wiser man, and one who had ac- cess to the best information, when he ventured to'expreef a hope that the depression that had so long hovered over them was at length slowly but steadily lifting, and that bet- ter days were in store for them, and that among other things which would make the advancing year memorable, and one of rejoicing and jubilee, would be the inaugura- tion of an era ef prosperity, that they might be able to set- tle their internal disorders, that the war clouds which were hovering over our continental neighbours might be dis- persed, that confidence might be restored and security given to capital, so that an impetus might be given to trade and enterprise, and that their unemployed might once more , return to happiness and contentment. (Applause.) The I chairman then referred to va-ious details of the balance sheet, and concluded by again moving the adoption of the report. —Mr. E. (Ingmar'. seconded the proposal, which was agreed to unanimously. I ... THE DIVIDEND.

Sir GILBERT GREENALL moved that, as recommended by the directors, a dividend for the past year, ending December 31st, at the rate of 15 per cent, per annum and a bonus of 10i per share be declared. both free of income tax.—aiptain WITHINGTON seconded this proposal, which was agreed to.

THE DIRECTORS' REMUNERATION. Mr. W. BEAMONT moved that the directors be thanked for the services they have rendered; that they be asked to con- tinue those services, and also that their remuneration be £5,000. He (Mr. Beamont) had been in hopes that he should have had to announce that this year was the second jubilee year of that bank as well as the jubilee of the reign of our present gracious sovereign, but he found that morn- ing in turning :o his bank beoks—of which he had a little library descended from his father—that the bank was one year younger than he thought it was. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) The book dated back to the year 1799, so that he was born before that book began. (Hear, hear.) At the time he referred to the shares in that bank were owned by three gentlemen, all of whom he had the pleasure to recol- lect, but now they had got a numerous family of share- holders, and it was pleasant to think that ia) raany gentle- men of ability were connected with that bank. 3he names of the three gentlemen who owned the shares in 179 D were Parr—a name with which they were still associated—Lyon, and Kerfoot. (Applanse.)—Mr. J. C. ECKERSLEY seconded the propoaal, and it was agreed to.

div.head: APPOINTMENTS.
div.p: APPOINTMENTS.

On the motion of Mr. R. PIERPOINT, the retiring direc- tors whose names are mentioned in the directors' report were re-elected.--It was also agreed to re-appoint Mr. J. C. Stead, accountant, Liverpool, as auditor Or the ensuing year at a salary of £4OO.

div.head: VOTES OF THANKS.
div.p: VOTES OF THANKS.

On the motion of Mr. H. S—riaz—v—o'N..—;.. vote of thanks was passed to the general manager of the bank, secretary, and other officers for their services during the past year.—Mr. Drew, the general manager, having acknowledged this vote, a similar compliment was paid to the chairman on the'mo• lion of Mr. R. DAVIES.—Mr. PARR having responded, the meeting concluded.

div.head: OPENING OF HAMILTON-STREET SCHOOLS.
div.p: OPENING OF HAMILTON-STREET SCHOOLS.

Oa Thursday evening the handsorne and commo- dious schools that have recently been. built in Hatnil- ton-street, off Battersby-lane, Warrington, were for- mally opened by the holding of a tea party, and a subsequent meeting, at which the Dean of Chester presided. When the scheme for building the school was originated, the Warrington Training Col- lege, being in need of practising schools, offered to contribute £1,600, provided they were permitted to use the schools, and that an additional 44430 was contributed. The money was soon forthcoming and the.work sei, in progress. Originally it was intended to provide accommodation for soo scholars, but the schools, as now completed, will accommodate about 650. The total cost of the building was about Li. 000. It is in the gothic style of architecture, and every con- venience has been provided. It is built of red briak, with, stone dressings. The joint architects for the , work were Mr. J. E. Wright and Mr. T. Beesley, of Warrington, and Mr. Gibson, of Warrington, WAB the builder. Nearly four hundred persons sat down to tea, and at the subsequent meeting there were among I those preSent, in addition to the Dean of Chester, the Revs. B. Wilkinson (vicar of St. Paul's), G. F Roberts (vicar of Hollinfare), W. H. Williams (vicar of Padgate) G. D. Wray (vicar of St. Peters), Canon Sharpe, and Mears. W. Beamont, J'. Fair- dough, R. Fairolough, J. E. Wright, R. W. Franoomb. Cawley, Smethurst, Jenkins, Moores, Booth, &o. The ladies' coaimittee consists of Mesdames Beamont, Stevenson, Langham, Woods, Bands, Venn, Cawley, R. Fakelough, Adams, Robin- son, Chrimee, Speakman, Smethurst, Goddard, Ferri- man, McFall, W. S. Woods, and the Misses Garnett, Whittle, and Joynson, many of whom were present. —The Dean of CHESTER, in opening the pi oceedings, said that it was believed that the schools would meet a great necessity in that neighbourhood. They had, however, a wider object. They would all know the old adage that "No chain is stronger than its weakest link," and really the educational effort throughout the whole of England must be viewed by those who were interested in it as depending one piece upon another. There had been something of a struggle in the few past years. The era of struggle, he thought, was somewhat over, and the mind of England was settling down again more to its old feeling. It was recognised now that all education that was really excellent must be based upon the religious culture of the children who were being instructed. There had been, no doubt, a time through which we had lately pass=Z, in which the intellectual development of our children had been too exulusively followed, and, just as when they were accustomed to fix their eyes on a particular point they lost sight of great issues on the right hand and on the left, it might be that the moral and religions capabilities of the children had not been developed quite as rapidly as the intellectual. He believed that there was what was commonly called a reaction on this point, and that England as England was determined that, for the present at least, the children should re• ceive relizious education, while not neglecting the development of their intellectual powers. He did not either believe that a child could be thoroughly well educated, even in a religious school, unless they did what they mull to develop both its moral and its in- tellectual capabilities. The pressure of competition in this land, which WRS perhaps running a little in excess, would not suffer the intellectual side of the country to be neglected. I.Jet all friends of the peo- ple, and of the people's children, take care that they had an excellent education in all its branches. Again, if they did not keep up the voluntary schools the rates would be increased, which was of moment to house- holders, although they kept up that system on a higher principle than that. The Dean asked those living in the neighbourhood to support the schools. Afterwards a few remarks were made by the Vicar of Padgate, and an entertainment followed. Amusing sketches were given by Mr. G. H. Hulme, of Manchester, and songs were contributed by Miss Monks. Messrs. R. Fairclough, W. H. Jenkins, E. Booth, and H, Archer. Mr. W. S. Woods presided at the piano.—At the conclusion a vote of thanks to those who had in any way assisted to add to the enjoyment of the even- ing was accorded on the motion of the Rev. M. STEVENSON, seconded by Mr. J. Ferantotron, and the Chairman was thanked for presiding, on the motion of Mr. Basmomr, seconded by the Dli.; S. mount- SON.
